Cell Isolation and in vitro assay  Neutrophil isolation was performed using magnetic-activated cell sorting (MACS) technology with species-specific markers, where mouse neutrophils were positively selected using Ly6G Microbeads (Miltenyi Biotec, 130–097-658) while human neutrophils were enriched via CD16 Microbeads (Miltenyi Biotec, 130–045-701), both achieving ≥90% purity as confirmed by flow cytometric analysis, with subsequent culture of the isolated cells in complete RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) under standard conditions. Both murine and human neutrophils were resuspended in Hank’s balanced saline solution (HBSS) containing 2% of bovine serum albumin (BSA) and calcium. Cell suspensions contained >95% of viable neutrophils, as established by flow cytometry. For coculture studies, MACS-sorted neutrophils were incubated with bladder cancer cells, with post-treatment fixation in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) and crystal violet (0.5%) staining for microscopic imaging analysis, while proliferation assays involved 96-hour incubation with CAP-activated medium followed by sulforhodamine B (SRB) colorimetric assessment performed per standard protocols.  Mouse neutrophils were isolated from female C57BL/6 mice (6–8 weeks old).  Human neutrophils were isolated from tumor specimens or peripheral blood of consented patients. After activating with CAP at 37°C and 5% CO 2 , neutrophils were washed in PBS and incubated with Mitophagy Dye (DOJINDO, MD01) or JC-1 dye (Beyotime Biotechnology, C2003S) for 30 min individually. Samples were washed twice in PBS and immediately analyzed by flow cytometry. The fluorescence of samples was measured in a flow cytometer and analyzed using FlowJo software. For flow cytometry, the following fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies were used: APC anti-human CD45 antibody (BioLegend, Cat# 304012, RRID: AB_314400), FITC anti-human CD66b antibody (BioLegend, Cat# 305104, RRID: AB_314496), FITC anti-mouse CD3 antibody (BioLegend, Cat# 100203, RRID: AB_312660), APC anti-mouse CD8a antibody (BioLegend, Cat# 100712, RRID: AB_312751), PerCP/Cy5.5 anti-human/mouse Granzyme B recombinant antibody (BioLegend, Cat# 372212, RRID: AB_2728379), APC anti-mouse/human CD11b antibody (BioLegend, Cat# 101212, RRID: AB_312795), PE anti-mouse Ly-6G antibody (BioLegend, Cat# 127607, RRID: AB_1186104).    Three-dimensional spheroid culture  Three-dimensional spheroid formation was achieved using an optimized hanging drop technique, wherein 15–30 μl aliquots of single-cell suspension containing 0.24% methylcellulose were carefully pipetted onto culture dish lids and inverted over PBS-filled base dishes to maintain humidity, followed by incubation under standard culture conditions (37°C, 5% CO 2 ) for 5 days with daily monitoring until aggregate formation; mature spheroids were then gently transferred to 96-well plates for confocal microscopic imaging at 10× magnification. While for neutrophil-bladder cancer cell coculture experiments, neutrophils were prelabeled with CFDA-SE [5(6)-carboxyfluorescein diacetate succinimidyl ester] fluorescent dye prior to spheroid formation to enable subsequent tracking and visualization.    ELISA  ELISA kits were used to assay the levels of mouse IL-12 (Cat: M3062; Elabscience), mouse TNF-α (Cat: M3063; Elabscience), and mouse IL-6 (Cat: M0044; Elabscience) in tumor tissue according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, the standard solution and samples were added to the plate and incubated for 2 hours at room temperature. Then, the wells were aspirated and washed 5 times with wash buffer, and the conjugate was added to each well followed by incubation for 2 hours. After five washes, the substrate solution and stop solution were added successively with a thorough mixture. The optical density of each well was determined using a microplate reader.    Analysis of OCR with the seahorse XF platform  To evaluate the oxygen consumption rate (OCR), neutrophils in Seahorse XF RPMI Medium without glucose (Agilent Technologies) were seeded in a 96-well XF Cell Culture Microplate (Agilent Technologies) pre-coated with poly-L-lysine. Cells were left to adhere for one hour at 37°C without CO 2 . Neutrophils were activated with CAP, and OCR were then measured on a Seahorse XF Analyser (Agilent Technologies) in basal conditions, and upon the sequential addition of oligomycin (1.5 μM), Carbonyl cyanide-4-(trifluoromethoxy)-phenylhydrazone (FCCP, 3 μM), and rotenone/antimycin A (1 μM).    Transcriptome sequencing (RNA-seq)  Mouse neutrophils were purified from tumors upon MACS cell sorting, and then neutrophils were treated with CAP and cocultured for 12 hours. Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent (Thermo Fisher, 15596018) following the manufacturer’s procedure. The total RNA quantity and purity were analyzed with a Bioanalyzer 2100 and RNA 6000 Nano LabChip Kit (Agilent, CA, USA, 5067–1511), and high-quality RNA samples with RIN > 7.0 were used to construct a sequencing library. After mRNA purification and cDNA amplification, we performed the 2× 150 bp paired-end sequencing (PE150) on an Illumina Novaseq 6000 (LC-Bio Technology CO., Ltd., Hangzhou, China) following the vendor’s recommended protocol. Gene differential expression analysis was performed by DESeq2 software between two different groups (and by edgeR between two samples). Genes with a false discovery rate (FDR) below 0.05 and absolute fold change ≥2 were considered differentially expressed genes.    Single-cell RNA-seq and data processing  Tumors from MB49-bearing mice with different treatment were digested in tissue dissociation solution according to the manufacturer’s instructions and single-cell suspensions were obtained. Tumor-infiltrating CD45 +  cells were enriched by FACS. Cell suspensions were counted with Countess 3 automated cell counter to determine cell concentration and viability. Cells were then loaded onto a microfluidic chip and scRNA-seq libraries were constructed according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The scRNA-seq libraries were sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq X10 instrument with 150 bp paired end reads. Raw sequencing reads were processed to generate gene expression profiles using CeleScope v1.5.2 (Singleron Biotechnologies) with default parameters. Adapters and polyA tails were trimmed before aligning reads to the mouse GRCm38. Reads with the same cell barcode, UMI, and gene were grouped together to generate the UMI count matrix.  Single-cell RNA-seq datasets ( GSE267718  and  GSE201425 ) were downloaded from the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). Only samples from patients with matched peripheral blood and tumor tissue scRNA-seq profiles were retained for subsequent analyses. Raw UMI count matrices were imported into R(v4.5.0) and analyzed using Seurat (v5.2.1). For each sample, seurat objects were created from raw UMI count matrices. Doublets were identified using the scDblFinder package (v1.24.0) and excluded from downstream analyses. Quality control filtering was applied to remove low-quality cells, retaining cells with nFeature_RNA > 500 and < 6000 and mitochondrial transcript fraction (percent.mt) < 25%. Then, data were normalized using SCTransform with default parameters. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed, and the top 30 PCs (dims = 1:30) were used for downstream analyses. To mitigate batch effects across samples, batch correction was carried out using the Harmony algorithm on the PCA embeddings.  After Harmony batch correction on the PCA space (dims = 1:30), we constructed the k-nearest neighbor graph using FindNeighbors (dims = 1:30) and performed graph-based clustering using FindClusters (resolution = 1.6 for  GSE267718  and 1.0 for  GSE201425 ). UMAP embeddings were generated using RunUMAP (dims = 1:30) for visualization. Differential gene expression analyses were performed using Seurat’s FindMarkers function with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test on the SCTransform-normalized expression values. Multiple testing correction was applied using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, and genes were considered differentially expressed if they met all of the following criteria: adjusted P value (padj) < 0.05, log2 fold change (log2FC) ≥ 1, and pct > 0.25. Cell types were annotated based on canonical marker gene expression. Heatmaps were visualized using ComplexHeatmap (v2.26.0).    Statistical analysis  Data analyses in the study were performed using GraphPad Prism. Figure legends specified the means and standard deviations, data presentation and statistical strategies, as well as all experimental repetitions and numbers of specimens. Two-tailed Student’s t-tests were used for two-group comparisons; one-way or two-way ANOVA for multiple groups; log-rank test for survival analyses; Wilcoxon rank-sum test for non-parametric data; RNA-seq analyses were performed using DESeq2 with FDR correction.  P  < 0.05 was considered as statistically significant (* P  < 0.05; ** P  < 0.01; *** P  < 0.001; **** P  < 0.0001). evidence_text:
InSituPy: a framework for histology-guided, multi-sample analysis of single-cell spatial omics data.

Motivation

Spatial omics data provides unprecedented insights into disease biology, yet its complexity introduces significant challenges in data analysis. Comprehensive analysis requires frameworks that integrate diverse modalities and enable joint processing of multiple datasets and corresponding metadata.

Results

To address these challenges, we introduce InSituPy, a versatile and scalable framework for analyzing spatial omics data from the multi-sample level down to the cellular and subcellular level. Its hierarchical data structure organizes all relevant data modalities per sample and links them to their corresponding metadata, enabling scalable analysis of large patient cohorts using spatial omics technologies. Interactive visualization tools within InSituPy enable seamless integration of histopathological expertise, promoting collaborative hypothesis generation in translational research. Additionally, InSituPy includes built-in analytical algorithms and interfaces with external tools, establishing a standardized workflow for multi-sample spatial omics data analysis.

Availability

The Python package InSituPy is publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/SpatialPathology/InSituPy) and PyPi (https://pypi.org/project/insitupy-spatial/), and archived on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18459471). Tutorials and documentation for InSituPy are available at https://insitupy.readthedocs.io/. All code to replicate the results shown in this manuscript can be found in the GitHub repository. Scripts to connect QuPath and InSituPy can be found at https://github.com/SpatialPathology/InSituPy-QuPath. All data required to complete the tutorials is publicly available, and functions to download the data have been implemented. A Zulip community chat for user support and discussion is accessible at https://insitupy.zulipchat.com.

Contact j.wirth@tum.de , katja.steiger@tum.de status released display-pdf yes is-olf no is-manuscript no is-preprint no is-journal-matter no is-scanned no is-retracted no Received 2025 Sep 5; Revised 2025 Dec 23; Accepted 2026 Jan 29; Collection date 2026 Mar. 1 Introduction The emergence of spatially resolved multi-omics technologies has the potential to revolutionize our understanding of biological processes in healthy and diseased tissue. While early methods such as Visium ( Ståhl et al. 2016 ) and Slide-seq ( Rodriques et al. 2019 ) measured transcriptomes within micron-sized spatial units and failed to achieve single cell resolution, the development of multiplexed fluorescence in situ hybridization (multiplexed FISH ) ( Lubeck et al. 2014 ; Xia et al. 2019 ) and in situ sequencing ( ISS ) ( Ke et al. 2013 ; Lee et al. 2014 ) allowed researchers to map individual RNA molecules at subcellular resolution and thus measure the transcriptional state of single cells within tissue sections. The non-destructive nature of multiplexed FISH and ISS technologies allows the combination of transcriptomic readouts with conventional image-based readouts such as histological or immunofluorescence stainings. Access to histological data enables full integration of pathological expert knowledge from routine diagnostics and opens new ways for hypothesis generation. Further, recent technologies such as Xenium in Situ (10X Genomics) and MERSCOPE (Vizgen) allow the analysis of multiple tissue sections at once, increasing the throughput of the methods and enabling the generation of large clinical cohorts, e.g. using tissue microarrays (TMAs). To fully exploit the potential of such datasets, it is important to integrate experiment-level information (e.g. clinical metadata or treatment conditions) with the single-cell spatial transcriptomics (scST) and proteomics (scSP) data. While Python -based frameworks such as SpatialData ( Marconato et al. 2025 ) allow an integration of spatial omics data modalities, they do not offer a way to structurally integrate data from multiple tissue sections or tissue microarrays with its corresponding metadata. Other tools such as ATHENA , MoleculeExperiment or SpatialExperiment provide strategies to integrate multiple samples but lack support for different aspects of the analysis, including integration of annotations, single transcript information, or interactive visualization, or are only available in R ( Martinelli and Rapsomaniki 2022 ; Righelli et al. 2022 ; Peters Couto et al. 2023 ). Additionally, since a growing number of researchers use spatial omics technologies in their projects, an easy usability, also for non-bioinformaticians, is key. In this publication, we present InSituPy , a Python-based framework to explore and analyze both single-cell and sequencing-based spatial omics data while simplifying and accelerating the preprocessing of multiple large datasets in parallel. Using published spatial transcriptomics datasets, we introduce workflows to perform multi-sample data analysis and integrate pathological expert knowledge into the analysis. 2 Results 2.1 Overall structure of the framework Single-cell spatial omics datasets consist of multiple data levels ( Fig. 1A ). These levels comprise (i) the experiment level, which can contain information about the patients, the model system or treatments; (ii) the sample level, containing all data of one data entity, e.g. one tissue section; (iii) a multi-cellular level with method-specific readouts (e.g. gene or protein expression) per spatial unit; (iv) the cellular level containing the readout per individual cell; and (v) the subcellular level including molecular information such as the location of individual transcripts. InSituPy offers a hierarchical and biologically meaningful data structure to read, analyze and store data from all those five levels ( Fig. 1B ). Divided into two main data objects, InSituExperiment and InSituData , the framework facilitates the integration of data from multiple tissue sections. An InSituExperiment object can store multiple InSituData objects, with each InSituData object containing the raw data, spatial omics modalities and, optionally, histological information of an individual sample ( Fig. 1B ). Each InSituData object gets assigned a unique ID (UID) to connect the datasets with its corresponding metadata, allowing different experiment-level operations, e.g. querying datasets based on their metadata, iterating through datasets or concatenating data from multiple experiments or visualization of individual datasets ( Fig. S1A-I , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). Further, information can be transferred between InSituExperiment objects and AnnData objects, allowing the creation of analysis loops between InSituPy and the scverse ecosystem, e.g. for batch correction ( Fig. S 1F , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). InSituPy is the first spatial omics analysis framework to introduce such a hierarchical data structure allowing both the handling of multiple datasets and a comprehensive analysis on the individual sample level as well as interactive visualization of the data ( Table S1 , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). Figure 1 Overview of InSituPy package structure and functionalities. (A) Data levels in spatial omics datasets. (B) Experiment- and sample-level data structure of the InSituExperiment and the InSituData classes. The InSituExperiment object stores multiple datasets with their corresponding metadata while the InSituData object structures data modalities into a biologically meaningful hierarchy. (C) Reading and writing streams within the InSituPy framework. Data can be loaded directly or via the spatialdata-io ecosystem ( Marconato et al . 2025 ). Data can be saved using the saveas function. On disk, the data is grouped into variable and static data. Variable data can be updated during analysis using the save function while static data remains unchanged to shorten writing times. Data modalities can be loaded separately using distinct load functions. (D) Schematic showing how histological annotations are grouped into annotations and regions. (E) Different possibilities to generate an InSituExperiment object. (F) Automated image registration workflow for aligning images of histological stainings acquired after the run with a fluorescent image that is already registered to the omics data. (G) Schematic showing possibilities to create multi-sample analysis workflows in InSituPy. Multiple internal analyses are available as well as interfaces connecting InSituPy to external analysis packages. Results can be plotted statically or visualized interactively through a napari-based viewer ( Sofroniew et al . 2024 ). 2.2 Data structure on sample level The sample level data structure of InSituPy ( InSituData ) is compatible with any spatially resolved omics data consisting of a count or abundance matrix, image data and optionally segmentation masks or transcript locations. Within an InSituData object, data is organized in six data categories: image data ( images ), transcript locations and identities ( transcripts ), omics data from arbitrarily shaped spatial units such as spots or tissue compartments ( units ), single-cell omics data ( cells ), histological annotations ( annotations ), and histological regions ( regions ) ( Fig. 1D ). While spatial units and cells both represent bounded areas with associated measurements, cells are treated independently as they possess unique properties including distinct nuclear and cellular boundaries. Both the cells and units attributes are further subdivided into layers, allowing integration of results from multiple cell segmentation algorithms or different types of spatial units. Each layer consists of two attributes: a table containing spatial omics data as an AnnData ( Virshup et al. 2021 ) object, paired with either a boundaries attribute storing nuclear and cellular segmentation masks (for cells ) or a shapes attribute containing polygons (for units ). Each data modality can be loaded individually using the respective loading functions ( Fig. 1C ). Image and transcript data is loaded lazily and only loading times for cellular data, annotations and regions increase with dataset size ( Fig. S2A , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). Analysis results can be saved in an InSituPy project folder. To optimize writing performance, the framework distinguishes between static data (i.e. data that remains unchanged during analysis such as raw image data and transcript locations) and variable data (i.e. data that is modified during analysis such as spatial omics data and histological data). When saving to an existing project, only variable data is written to disk, significantly reducing save times ( Fig. S2B , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). For data handling, the framework uses different state-of-the-art packages ( Table S2 , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). In case of histological data, InSituPy differentiates between regions and annotations ( Fig. 1B and D ). Annotations can be any histological annotation (e.g. “tumor”), while regions are meant to delineate the positions of TMA cores or different tissue sections within the same dataset. 2.3 Multi-sample and multi-modal data assembly InSituExperiment objects can be assembled using three strategies ( Fig. 1E ): (i) from histological regions, e.g. TMA cores; (ii) from individual InSituData objects; (iii) from a configuration file containing data directories and corresponding metadata. For transcriptomic methods such as Xenium In Situ and Visium, dedicated reading functions and alignment tools are implemented, facilitating the joint analysis of single-cell and spot-based spatial omics approaches ( Fig. S3A , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). Further, technology-agnostic import workflows are documented, enabling integration of additional platforms. For spatial proteomic technologies based on multiplex immunofluorescence (e.g. co-detection by indexing ( Schürch et al. 2020 )), a technology-agnostic workflow using QuPath ( Bankhead et al. 2017 ) and InstanSeg ( Goldsborough et al. 2024 ) has been implemented. This workflow enables import of one or more samples into InSituPy ( Fig. S3B , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). In addition, functionality to quantify immunofluorescence signal intensity per cell from aligned images has been implemented as well ( Fig. S3C , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). The quantification algorithm processes images in tiles, avoiding full image loading into memory and enabling analysis on standard hardware with limited RAM ( Fig. S3D , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). 2.4 Interoperability with SpatialData To ensure interoperability with analysis packages from the scverse ecosystem ( Virshup et al. 2023 ), InSituPy provides bidirectional conversion functions between InSituData or InSituExperiment objects and the SpatialData format ( Fig. S4 , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). While SpatialData’s flat, keyword-based structure offers flexibility, it can become unwieldy when working with complex, multi-modal datasets. InSituPy addresses this limitation through a hierarchical data structure that provides organized access to different data modalities and improves scalability for larger datasets. In addition, the conversion functions provide access to spatialdata-io readers, extending InSituPy’s compatibility to technologies beyond its native readers. Benchmarking the InSituPy Xenium reader against its spatialdata-io counterpart revealed that spatialdata-io required substantially longer reading times and higher memory consumption, making it difficult to load very large datasets on normal computers and highlighting the advantage of technology-specialized readers over more generalized ones. 2.5 Automated image registration The non-destructive nature of spatial omics methods such as Xenium or CODEX ( Black et al. 2021 ) enables the subsequent histological staining of sections. To simplify integration of pathological annotations, InSituPy provides an automated registration pipeline that aligns the nuclear image acquired during the spatial omics measurement with subsequently stained images ( Fig. 1F ). The pipeline employs Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) to identify features in both images ( Lowe 2004 ), followed by the Fast Library for Approximate Nearest Neighbors (FLANN) for feature matching ( Muja and Lowe 2009 ). The random sample consensus algorithm (RANSAC) then selects the most robust feature matches to calculate an affine or perspective transformation matrix for image registration. Registered images are saved alongside quality control metrics and integrated into the InSituData object for downstream analysis. 2.6 Data visualization and annotation using the InSituPy viewer A precise registration of the images is a prerequisite for the addition of histological annotations to the datasets and for visualizing the results of the single-cell spatial omics analyses in their histopathological context. This is particularly important for morphological quality control and for leveraging the translational potential of spatial omics analyses. Histological annotations can be either imported from external software such as QuPath ( Bankhead et al. 2017 ) or from a napari-based viewer ( Sofroniew et al. 2024 ) ( Fig. S5 , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). The viewer provides various functionalities for data examination, including visualization of spatial omics data and cellular boundaries, localization of specific cells, and adding and displaying annotations or regions ( Figs. S5 and S6 , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). Added regions or annotations can be synchronized with the source InSituData object via a dedicated button. In case of multi-sample datasets stored as InSituExperiment object, individual datasets can be visualized and annotated in parallel. 2.7 Data analysis using InSituPy Leveraging the InSituExperiment object structure, InSituPy facilitates multi-sample analysis workflows through simple and streamlined syntax. Analyses can be performed within or between samples, and depending on the biological question, can be focused on specific regions, annotations, or cell types ( Fig. 1G ). Currently available analyses include cellular composition evaluation, the measurement of cell type densities, differential gene expression analysis and pseudobulk analysis. Further, InSituPy offers interfaces to external tools such as STRING, Enrichr and g:Profiler for GO term enrichment analysis, decoupler for enrichment analysis, and squidpy for spatial analyses ( Kuleshov et al. 2016 ; Raudvere et al. 2019 ; Szklarczyk et al. 2019 ; Badia-i-Mompel et al. 2022 ; Palla et al. 2022 ). Since omics data is stored in the AnnData format, all scverse functions are expected to be compatible with InSituPy. Further, InSituPy provides plotting functionalities to visualize the results of multi-sample datasets ( Fig. S1H , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). Together, these functionalities allow a histomorphology-informed analysis of gene expression changes in multi-sample spatial omics datasets. A complete step-by-step analysis has been demonstrated using published breast cancer Xenium In Situ data ( Janesick et al. 2023 ) and revealed differentially expressed genes within one cancer cell subtype between different histological regions ( Supplementary Methods and Figs. S7 and S8 , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). In addition, we provide a tutorial on how to import previously published data of a pulmonary fibrosis TMA (Vannan et al. 2025) into an InSituExperiment object and perform preprocessing steps ( Fig. S9 , available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online ). 3 Discussion In this work, we introduce InSituPy, a comprehensive Python-based framework, designed to simplify the handling, analysis, and visualization of multi-sample spatial omics data. While state-of-the-art Python-based analysis frameworks such as SpatialData ( Marconato et al. 2025 ) or Squidpy ( Palla et al. 2022 ) focus on a sample-level analysis, InSituPy allows handling of data at both the sample and experiment levels. With functions to read, write, query and analyze the datasets, InSituPy lays the foundation for large spatial omics projects, including multiple tissue sections or tissue microarrays from large patient cohorts. For the multi-sample analysis of such datasets, InSituPy provides functionalities to conduct analysis within and across samples using a simple syntax. On a sample level, currently published frameworks such as SpatialData structure the data based on the geometric properties of the modalities, e.g. as shapes or points. In contrast, InSituPy introduces a hierarchical data structure which groups the modalities into biologically meaningful layers, making analyses more intuitive and more accessible for non-bioinformaticians and medical experts. To allow interoperability between both frameworks, we implemented bidirectional conversion functions, giving InSituPy users access to data analysis workflows developed for SpatialData. In the future, we aim to further strengthen the support of SpatialData while also introducing advanced data formats for metadata handling such as ehrapy ( Heumos et al. 2024 ). A central step in the analysis of spatial omics data is the alignment of concurrently generated image data, which often requires laborious manual steps. Based on previously published analysis pipelines ( Wirth et al. 2023 ) and similarly to R-based tools like VoltRon ( Manukyan et al. 2023 ), InSituPy uses the computer vision toolbox OpenCV to facilitate an efficient and automated alignment of images from histological or immunofluorescent stainings. To verify results and develop hypotheses during analysis, interactive visualization of the data is crucial. Based on the napari framework ( Sofroniew et al. 2024 ), InSituPy offers visualization of image data and cellular omics data of multiple datasets as well as the handling of histological annotations or regions, facilitating the integration of pathological expert knowledge and opening new ways of generating hypotheses and driving translational research. All functionalities were demonstrated on a Xenium In Situ breast cancer dataset; however, InSituPy’s data structure is suitable for all types of imaging-based and sequencing-based spatial transcriptomics as well as spatial proteomics methodologies. Technology-agnostic data import strategies are available and explained in the documentation. Furthermore, InSituPy supports bidirectional conversion with SpatialData objects, enabling data import from various spatial omics technologies through the spatialdata-io ecosystem while maintaining InSituPy’s biology-inspired hierarchical structure for downstream analysis. Notably, benchmarking of InSituPy’s native Xenium reader against its spatialdata-io counterpart also highlights that specialized readers optimized for specific data formats can significantly improve loading performance. In conclusion, InSituPy represents the first Python-based framework for multi-sample spatial omics analysis that seamlessly integrates sample-level and experiment-level data handling. Through its biology-inspired hierarchical structure and comprehensive documentation, InSituPy establishes standardized analysis workflows that improve accessibility for non-bioinformaticians and disease experts. Malignant epithelial states drive immune dysfunction in ampulla of Vater carcinoma.

Background

Ampulla of Vater (AoV) carcinoma is a rare malignancy arising at the junction of intestinal and pancreatobiliary epithelium. Its heterogeneous clinical behavior and histological diversity have hindered therapeutic advances, and the cellular basis of this heterogeneity remains unclear. We aimed to construct a single-cell transcriptomic atlas of AoV carcinoma, with a focus on identifying epithelial subtypes and their interactions with the tumor microenvironment (TME).

Methods

We performed single-cell RNA sequencing on eight primary AoV tumors and four matched normal tissues. Comprehensive clustering and transcriptomic analyses identified cell-type composition, epithelial heterogeneity, and tumor-immune interactions. Findings were validated using deconvolution of bulk RNA-seq data from 62 AoV carcinoma patients. Results Malignant epithelial cells were categorized into four distinct subtypes: Int-Wnt, PB-KRAS, Int-Hypoxia, and Cycling stage. PB-KRAS cells exhibited stem-like transcriptional programs and high genomic instability. Deconvolution analysis of bulk RNA-seq data from the independent AoV cohort revealed that enrichment of the PB-KRAS subtype correlated with tumor recurrence and poor survival. Our immune profiling analysis discovered a significant association between PB-KRAS subtype and GZMK+ CD8+ T cells, which are in a pre-dysfunctional state, alongside SPP1+ macrophages exhibiting immunosuppressive traits. Spatial transcriptome data further supports the immunosuppressive natures of TME around PB-KRAS subtype malignant epithelial cells in AoV carcinoma.

Conclusions

Our study presents a single-cell atlas of AoV carcinoma, highlighting the molecular diversity of malignant epithelium and its association with the immune microenvironment. The PB-KRAS subtype emerges as a stem-like, immunosuppressive tumor state associated with poor prognosis, providing insights for future therapeutic targeting. Background Ampulla of Vater (AoV) carcinoma is a malignancy arising from the ampulla of Vater, the anatomical convergence of the common bile duct, pancreatic duct, and duodenum. This unique anatomical location gives rise to both histological and molecular heterogeneity, reflecting contributions from intestinal and pancreatobiliary lineages. AoV carcinoma is often categorized into intestinal and pancreatobiliary subtypes, which exhibit distinct prognostic and therapeutic characteristics [ 1 , 2 ]. However, this binary classification does not fully account for the molecular diversity and variable clinical behavior observed among patients [ 3 ]. Previous genomic studies have provided important insights into the molecular landscape of AoV carcinoma. Notably, Yachida et al. [ 4 ] identified frequent mutations in the ELF3 gene, implicating it as a potential driver of tumorigenesis. Similarly, Gingras et al. [ 5 ] reported recurrent ELF3 inactivation and widespread dysregulation of the WNT signaling pathway. While these studies advanced our understanding of AoV carcinogenesis, they were based on whole-exome sequencing and bulk transcriptome profiling, which lack the resolution to capture cell type-specific transcriptional programs and the complexity of tumor-microenvironment interactions. As a result, the biological basis of epithelial heterogeneity and the functional contributions of non-malignant cell populations remain poorly understood. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) offers a powerful approach to address these limitations by enabling high-resolution, cell-type-resolved transcriptomic profiling [ 6 ]. This technology facilitates the identification of cellular subpopulations, and intercellular communication networks that are not accessible through bulk sequencing methods. Despite its potential, scRNA-seq has not yet been applied to AoV carcinoma, leaving fundamental gaps in our understanding of its cellular and transcriptional architecture. Therefore, our study is essential to move beyond bulk-level genomic insights and establish a high-resolution, cell-type-resolved atlas of AoV carcinoma. In this study, we present the first single-cell transcriptomic analysis of AoV carcinoma. Using scRNA-seq on primary tumor specimens, we identify distinct epithelial subtypes characterized by unique oncogenic and reveal their associations with the immune landscape and clinical outcomes. This work establishes a foundational single-cell atlas of AoV carcinoma and provides new insights into its cellular diversity with potential translational implications. Methods Study patients This study included 70 patients histologically diagnosed with AoV adenocarcinoma between September 2005 and March 2023 at Samsung Medical Center (SMC), of whom eight underwent single-cell RNA sequencing and 62 underwent bulk RNA sequencing. Patient demographics and clinical characteristics, including age, gender, tumor stage according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 8th edition, tumor differentiation, adjuvant chemotherapy administration, and survival data, were retrospectively collected. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board at SMC (IRB No. SMC-2022–06-076) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. All participants provided written informed consent for the future research use of their pathology specimens. Single-cell RNA sequencing Fresh tumor and adjacent normal tissue specimens were obtained from patients with AoV carcinoma before treatment through Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) for scRNA sequencing. Acquired tissues are collected in MACS® Tissue Storage Solution (Miltenyi Biotec., Auburn, CA, USA) on ice and processed to the single cell dissociation immediately. Biopsy tissues are placed on a petri dish with a small volume of enzyme mixture solution (Tumor Dissociation Kit, Miltenyi Biotec.) and minced into small pieces under 1–2 mm with surgical blades. Minced pieces are transferred to gentleMACS TM C-tube containing enzyme mixture solution. By choosing an appropriate program of gentleMACS TM Dissociator, tissue pieces are further dissociated three times with two interval incubations for 30 minutes at 37 °C under continuous rotation using the MACSmix TM Tube Rotator. Resuspended samples are applied to a cell strainer (70 μm) and washed with 10 ml of DMEM/F12 media with 1% FBS. After a centrifugation at 400xg for 5 minutes, cells were resuspended in an appropriate volume of media and counted with trypan blue staining or acridine orange/propidium iodide staining. Optionally, erythrocytes are removed by red blood cell lysis solution for 10 min before counting. We initiated the cell preparation process by employing the LUNA-FL™ Automated Fluorescence Cell Counter (logos biosystems). Detailed guidelines for cell preparation were sourced from the 10x Genomics Single Cell Protocols Cell Preparation Guide and the Guidelines for Optimal Sample Preparation flowchart. Libraries were meticulously constructed using the Chromium controller in accordance with the 10x Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3’ v3.1 protocol (10x Genomics). In brief, cell suspensions were diluted in nuclease-free water, aiming to achieve a targeted cell count of 10,000. The diluted cell suspension was mixed with a master mix and subsequently loaded onto a Chromium Next GEM chip, along with Single Cell 3’ V3.1 gel beads and partitioning oil. Within the droplets formed in the chip, RNA transcripts from individual cells underwent unique barcoding and reverse transcription. Pooled cDNA molecules then underwent sequential processes, including end repair, addition of a single ‘A’ base, and adapter ligation. Subsequently, the resulting products were subjected to purification and enrichment through polymerase chain reaction (PCR), ultimately yielding the final cDNA library. To ensure library quality and quantify the purified libraries, we adhered to the qPCR Quantification Protocol Guide (KAPA). Furthermore, library qualification was performed using the Agilent Technologies 4200 TapeStation from Agilent Technologies. The sequenced libraries were processed using the HiSeqX platform from Illumina to obtain the requisite data for our study. Data preprocessing and quality control Raw sequencing data were processed using CellRanger (v7.0.1; 10x Genomics) [ 7 ], with alignment to the GRCh38 reference genome via STAR. CellBender (v 0.2.2) [ 8 ] was applied to each sample to eliminate background RNA contamination. Doublets were detected using Scrublet (v 0.2.3) [ 9 ], with thresholds determined according to simulation-derived scores. we excluded low-quality cells with fewer than 500 detected genes and a mitochondrial gene proportion exceeding 20%. Seurat (v4.3.0) [ 10 ] was used for downstream processing, including normalization, variable gene selection, scaling (regressing out total UMI counts, mitochondrial gene proportion, and cell cycle scores), principal component analysis, and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) projection. Clustering was performed using the FindNeighbors and FindClusters functions, with dimensionality assessed via JackStraw and ElbowPlot methods. Cell type annotation was conducted using SingleR (v2.0.0) [ 11 ] and further validated through the expression of canonical lineage markers. Major cell types were identified using EPCAM (epithelial cells), COL1A1 (fibroblasts), VWF (endothelial cells), CD3D (T cells), CD14 (myeloid cells), and CD79A (B cells). For more granular annotation of immune and stromal subsets, we utilized the following marker sets: CD4 for helper T cells, CD8 for cytotoxic T cells, FOXP3 for regulatory T cells (Tregs), and NCAM1 and NCR1 for NK cells. Myeloid sub-populations were defined by C1QC (macrophages), LYZ and S100A9 (monocytes), CD1C (dendritic cells), and CPA3 and KIT (mast cells). B cell lineages were further distinguished using CD79A and MS4A1 (B cells), CD38 and CD27 (plasma cells). Subclustering analyses were performed on major immune and stromal compartments following additional doublet removal [ 12 ]. Identification of epithelial subtypes using cNMF To identify transcriptional programs within epithelial cells, we applied consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF) (v0.2) [ 13 ] to the normalized gene expression matrix. The number of components (k) was varied from 2 to 15, and the optimal solution was selected based on silhouette scores and Frobenius reconstruction error. Copy number variation inference To infer copy number alterations at the single-cell level, CopyKAT (v1.1.0) [ 14 ] was applied with default parameters. T cells were used as a reference for normal diploid profiles. CNV scores were computed for individual epithelial cells and summarized across samples to evaluate subtype-specific genomic instability. Transcription factor regulatory network inference Regulatory network analysis was performed using the pySCENIC (v0.12.1) [ 15 ] pipeline. Regulon activity scores were computed from raw UMI matrices to identify transcription factor-target gene modules, and average activity scores were calculated per subtype for downstream comparative analyses. Modular score and stemness estimation The CytoTRACE algorithm (v0.3.3) [ 16 ] was used to infer the differentiation potential of malignant epithelial cells. CytoTRACE computes transcriptional diversity and expression correlation to derive stemness scores, ranging from 0 (fully differentiated) to 1 (highly undifferentiated). This approach enables the identification of less differentiated, stem-like cell states at single-cell resolution. To evaluate functional characteristics of epithelial subtypes, including stemness potential, we calculated gene module scores using AddModuleScore function in the Seurat package. This approach determines the average expression of a specific gene program at the single-cell level, which is then normalized by subtracting the aggregated expression of control feature sets. To ensure a robust baseline, all analyzed features are binned based on their average expression levels, and control features are randomly selected from each bin. This process effectively accounts for technical noise and the influence of overall gene expression profiles. The stemness gene set was constructed using previously reported stemness-associated markers [ 17 ]. Functional enrichment analysis Differentially expressed genes were selected based on adjusted p -values and fold changes. Functional enrichment analysis was performed using EnrichR (v3.2) [ 18 ], employing the hypergeometric test with default parameters to identify overrepresented pathways and biological processes. We employed the hypergeometric test with default parameters to identify overrepresented pathways and biological processes from the MSigDB Hallmark gene set collection. Cell-cell communication analysis Ligand-receptor interaction analysis was conducted using CellPhoneDB (v5.0.0) [ 19 ] to identify potential intercellular communication events between cell types. Significant interactions were inferred via permutation testing using default parameters. Pseudotime trajectory analysis To infer the developmental hierarchy of epithelial subtypes, we performed pseudotime trajectory analysis using the Monocle2 R package (v2.30.0) [ 20 ]. To minimize potential biological variations across patients, we utilized the integrated data generated via the FindIntegrationAnchors and IntegrateData functions from the Seurat package. For trajectory ordering, we selected the top 30 differentially expressed genes from each epithelial cluster. Dimensionality reduction was performed using the DDRTree algorithm. Bulk RNA sequencing and processing For bulk RNA sequencing, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor tissues from an independent cohort of surgically resected 62 AoV carcinoma patients were analyzed. Transcript-level quantification was achieved using RSEM (v1.3.0) [ 21 ], aligned to the GRCh38 genome with GENCODE v33 annotation. Gene-level expression matrices were derived for integrative analyses with single-cell data. Proportions of each subtype were estimated in bulk RNA-seq samples using MuSiC (v1.0.0) [ 22 ]. Xenium in situ hybridization and spatial analysis Surgically resected FFPE tissue samples from AoV tumor patients were profiled using Xenium Prime 5K Human Pan Tissue and Pathways Panel (10x Genomics). FFPE tissue sections (5 µm) were prepared on Xenium slides using Xenium Prime Sample Preparation Reagents. RNA quality was assessed by calculating the percentage of RNA fragments > 200 nucleotides (DV200) extracted from tissue sections, and H&E staining were also used to assess tissue morphology and region of interests by a specialized pathologist before performing the Xenium in situ hybridization. Slides were deparaffinized, rehydrated and decrosslinked, followed by hybridization with Xenium 5K Priming Oligos and probes targeting messenger RNA. Probes were ligated, amplified and washed, with subsequent antibody staining for cell segmentation. Autofluorescence quenching and nuclei staining were performed and slides they were stored in phosphate-buffered saline with tween-20 (PBS-T) at 4 °C. The Xenium Analyzer (version 3.1) was used for imaging, decoding, segmentation and cell assignment, following the manufacturer’s protocols. During the initial quality control and filtering step, cells with a transcript count below 100 were classified as low-quality and excluded from all downstream analyses. For cell type classification, we utilized our own scRNA-seq dataset as the reference. Cell assignment was performed using the FindTransferAnchors and TransferData functions within the Seurat package, employing default parameters. Cells with a prediction score below 0.5 were classified as unknown and excluded from further downstream analyses. Survival analysis The clinical relevance of epithelial subtypes was evaluated using survival analysis. Kaplan-Meier curves were generated using the survival and survminer R packages (v0.5.2). Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression models were implemented using the coxph function to assess associations with overall survival and disease-free survival. Statistical analysis All statistical analyses were performed in R. Pair-wise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests were utilized to analyze the proportional differences between groups within each cell type/subset. Significance is displayed as *, p  < 0.05; **, p  < 0.01; and ***, p  < 0.001. For comparisons among multiple groups, the Kruskal-Wallis test was used to determine global significance, followed by Dunn’s test for pairwise post-hoc comparisons with adjustments for multiple testing. Statistical significance for multiple comparisons is presented as adjusted p -values (Padj), indicated as follows: *, Padj < 0.05;, Padj < 0.01; and ***, Padj < 0.001. Pearson correlation was employed to calculate the correlation between the proportions of each pair of cell subsets, and Spearman correlation was used for the co-ecosystem analysis. Results Patient characteristics This study included 70 patients (scRNA-seq: n  = 8 and bulk RNA-seq: n  = 62) with AoV carcinoma. Median age was 61.5 years (range, 36–83 years) and 33 were male (47.1%). Tumor stage (AJCC 8th edition) was I-III in the majority of patients (67/70, 95.7%), with only one patient classified as stage 0 and two as stage IV. During a median follow-up of 9.7 years (interquartile range, 6.4–12.7 years), 27 deaths (38.6%) occurred (Table S1 ). Single-cell transcriptomic profiling reveals diverse cellular composition in AoV carcinoma To investigate the cellular architecture of AoV carcinoma, we performed scRNA-seq on tumors ( n  = 8) and matched adjacent normal tissues ( n  = 4) (Fig. 1 a). After quality filtering, a total of 34,672 cells were analyzed and grouped into 18 clusters, which were subsequently classified into six major cell types based on cell type marker gene expression (Fig. 1 b–c). UMAP visualization revealed that while immune cells were broadly shared across patients, epithelial cell clusters displayed strong patient-specific transcriptional profiles, consistent with the absence of batch effects and reflecting inter-patient variation driven by tumor-specific copy number alterations [ 23 , 24 ] (Fig. 1 d). We further examined the distribution of cell types across individual samples, revealing substantial inter-patient heterogeneity in cellular composition (Fig. 1 e). Some tumors were highly enriched in epithelial or myeloid populations, whereas others showed greater T cell infiltration. These findings highlight the cellular complexity of AoV carcinoma and underscore the diversity of tumor-immune microenvironments across patients. Fig. 1 Single-cell transcriptomic profiling of ampulla of Vater (AoV) carcinoma tissues. ( a ) Schematic overview of the study design. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was performed on 8 AoV tumor samples and 4 matched normal tissues. Bulk RNA-seq data from 62 AoV samples were also generated. ( b ) Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) visualization of major cell types identified in scRNA-seq data. Cells are colored by their annotated cell type: B cell, endothelial cell, epithelial cell, fibroblast, myeloid, and T cell. ( c ) Feature plots showing expression of representative marker genes for each major cell type: EPCAM (epithelial), COL1A1 (fibroblast), VWF (endothelial), CD3D (T cell), CD14 (myeloid), and CD79A (B cell). Expression levels are indicated by color intensity. ( d ) UMAP plot of scRNA-seq data color-coded by individual patient. ( e ) Estimated cell-type proportions in scRNA-seq data across tumor ( T ) and matched normal ( N ) samples for each patient, based on annotation from ( b ). Bar plots display relative proportions of each major cell type Epithelial subtyping reveals distinct transcriptional programs and inter-patient heterogeneity To investigate epithelial heterogeneity in AoV carcinoma, we performed subclustering of epithelial cells. This analysis revealed strong patient-specific clustering patterns (Fig. 2 a), indicating pronounced transcriptional differences between tumors. We then applied consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF) to the epithelial transcriptomes, identifying four robust molecular subtypes (NMF-1 to NMF-4) (Fig. S1 a-b). Although each subtype included epithelial cells from multiple patients, their relative proportions varied markedly across samples (Fig. 2 b). This suggests that, while certain transcriptional programs are shared among tumors, their dominance is highly patient-specific, reflecting substantial inter-patient heterogeneity. Fig. 2 Identification and characterization of transcriptional subtypes in AoV carcinoma. ( a ) UMAP visualization of epithelial cells from AoV tissues ( n  = 8), color-coded by patient sample. ( b ) Proportional composition of four transcriptional subtypes (NMF-1 to NMF-4) in each AoV tumor, identified by consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF) clustering of epithelial transcriptomes. ( c ) Violin plots showing expression levels of well-known marker genes associated with AoV subtypes: CDX2 and KRT20 (intestinal subtype), MUC1 and KRT7 (pancreatobiliary subtype). ( d ) Functional enrichment analysis of each transcriptional subtype, visualized as a bubble plot. The pathways were identified using the MSigDB hallmark gene set collection. The size of each dot represents the statistical significance (-log 10 adjusted p -value), and the color denotes the corresponding transcriptional subtype We further examined the expression of established AoV subtype marker genes across the four subtypes (Fig. 2 c). Intestinal markers ( CDX2 and KRT20 ) were strongly expressed in NMF-1 and NMF-3, whereas pancreatobiliary markers ( KRT7 and MUC1 ) were predominantly enriched in NMF-2. These findings support the biological relevance of the identified subtypes and their alignment with previously described histological features [ 2 , 25 ]. Functional enrichment analysis revealed distinct transcriptional programs characterizing each subtype (Fig. 2 d and Table S2 ): NMF-1 was enriched for Wnt/β-catenin signaling (designated Int-Wnt), NMF-2 for KRAS signaling (PB-KRAS), NMF-3 for hypoxia-related pathways (Int-Hypoxia), and NMF-4 for cell cycle-associated signatures (Cycling). We categorize these four programs as three lineage-driven, differentiated subtypes and one progenitor/functional subtype (NMF-4, Cycling). To further characterize the regulatory landscape underlying epithelial heterogeneity, we performed regulon activity analysis across epithelial cells. This analysis revealed that multiple transcription factor regulons were differentially activated in a subtype-specific manner (Fig. S1 c). MSX1 activity was predominantly elevated in the Int-Wnt subtype compared to the PB-KRAS and Cycling subtypes. HNF1B activity reached its highest levels in the PB-KRAS subtype, showing a significant increase over the Cycling subtype and a strong upward trend compared to the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtypes. SIRT6 activity was notably enriched in the Int-Hypoxia subtype, while CDX1 was most active in the Cycling subtype, significantly surpassing the levels in the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia groups (Fig. S1 d). The MSX1 is a known WNT/β-catenin responsive transcription factor implicated in promoting intestinal tumorigenesis [ 26 ]. Similarly, the enrichment of HNF1B in the PB-KRAS subtype is relevant, as its overexpression has been shown to enhance the expression of liver progenitor cell markers and stemness in liver cancer cells [ 27 ]. Finally, the activation of the SIRT6 regulon in the Int-Hypoxia subtype is consistent with its known role in enhancing the stability of HIF-1α, a process linked to epithelial-mesenchymal transition under hypoxic conditions [ 28 ]. These regulon profiles were concordant with the transcriptional programs defined by cNMF, further supporting the molecular distinction among AoV epithelial subtypes. Collectively, these results demonstrate that epithelial cells in AoV carcinoma exhibit diverse transcriptional states driven by lineage-specific and oncogenic programs, with subtype composition varying substantially between tumors. PB-KRAS subtype exhibit distinct genomic instability and stem-like properties To interrogate the degree of genomic instability underlying each epithelial subtype, we first analyzed copy number variation (CNV) profiles inferred from single-cell transcriptomes. Notably, CNV patterns were strongly patient-specific, indicating inter-patient variability in genomic alterations (Fig. 3 a). At the single-cell level, CNV scores were markedly elevated in tumor epithelial cells compared to non-epithelial controls, with the PB-KRAS subtype exhibiting the highest levels of genomic aberrations (Fig. S2 a). To validate these findings at the sample level, we averaged CNV scores across epithelial cells within each sample and compared them across subtypes. This analysis confirmed that the PB-KRAS subtype exhibits the highest CNV burden among all epithelial subtypes (Kruskal-Wallis, p  = 0.00013; Fig. 3 b). These results indicate that genomic instability is unevenly distributed among AoV epithelial subtypes and is particularly pronounced in PB-KRAS subtype. For pairwise post-hoc comparisons, Dunn’s test was used to adjust for multiple comparisons. *Padj < 0.05, ** Padj < 0.01, *** Padj < 0.001; n.s., not significant Given that high genomic instability is frequently associated with aggressive phenotypes and enhanced self-renewal capacity [ 29 ], we next investigated the functional and developmental hierarchy of these subtypes. Based on its highest CNV burden, we specifically focused on evaluating the stem-like properties of the PB-KRAS subtype. We first focused on the Cycling subtype. Given its cell cycle-associated transcriptional program and the enrichment of progenitor-associated regulons, such as CDX1 (Fig. S1 d), we hypothesized that it represents a less differentiated, progenitor-like state. To infer the developmental potential across all subtypes, we employed CytoTRACE [ 16 ], a computational tool that infers developmental potential using transcriptional entropy. As expected, the Cycling subtype exhibited high CytoTRACE scores (Fig. 3 c and Fig. S2 b), supporting its identity as a less differentiated, progenitor-like state. Surprisingly, the PB-KRAS subtype, which otherwise presents as a differentiated lineage, exhibited the highest CytoTRACE scores (Fig. 3 c and Fig. S2 b), suggesting unexpected stem-like features. This combination—a seemingly differentiated state with high developmental potential—defines a non-canonical stemness phenotype. This suggests that, unlike the canonical progenitor-like Cycling subtype, the PB-KRAS subtype represents a distinct, highly aggressive stem-like epithelial state that deviates from the typical differentiation pathway. To further examine this possibility, we calculated stemness scores based on a curated stem cell gene signature [ 17 ]. The PB-KRAS subtype exhibited elevated stemness scores that were comparable to those of Cycling cells, while remaining notably higher than the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtypes (Kruskal-Wallis, p  = 0.00043; Fig. 3 d and Fig. S2 c). To provide dynamic evidence of this developmental hierarchy, we performed pseudotime trajectory analysis using Monocle2 [ 20 ]. The resulting trajectory delineated a clear lineage progression originating from the Cycling subtype, passing through the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtype, and ultimately culminating in the PB-KRAS subtype at the terminal end (Fig. 3 e). Notably, despite its terminal position on the pseudotime axis—which typically denotes a fully differentiated state—the PB-KRAS subtype harbored exceptionally high developmental potential, consistent with its elevated CytoTRACE (Fig. 3 f) and stemness scores (Fig. 3 g). This paradoxical terminal stemness suggests that PB-KRAS cells do not merely follow a conventional differentiation path but may undergo a coordinated transcriptional reprogramming or de-differentiation process, re-acquiring progenitor-like properties at an advanced stage of lineage development. We next sought to determine the potential molecular drivers of this phenotype, focusing on KRAS , the defining feature of the PB-KRAS subtype. Expression of KRAS was significantly upregulated in PB-KRAS subtype compared to the Int-Wnt subtypes (Fig. 3 h and Fig. S2 d), whereas CNV at the KRAS locus showed no significant difference among the subtypes (Fig. 3 i). Consistent with this, correlation analysis at the sample level revealed a moderate positive correlation between CNV score and stemness score ( r  = 0.5, p  = 0.014, Fig. S2 e). Furthermore, the expression of KRAS showed a strong positive correlation with both stemness score ( r  = 0.6, p  = 0.002, Fig. S2 f) and CNV score ( r  = 0.59, p  = 0.002, Fig. S2 g). These findings collectively highlight the robust association of both genomic instability and KRAS expression with the enhanced stem-like properties of the PB-KRAS subtype. Since KRAS knockdown in pancreatic cancer cells is known to reduce stemness characteristics [ 30 ], these observations suggest that the transcriptional upregulation of KRAS , rather than genomic alterations, is the likely contributor to the stemness signature of the PB-KRAS subtype. Epithelial subtypes confer distinct prognostic significance and clinical relevance in AoV carcinoma To evaluate the clinical significance of the four epithelial subtypes (Int-Wnt, PB-KRAS, Int-Hypoxia, and Cycling), we first deconvoluted their proportions in bulk RNA-seq profiles from 62 AoV carcinoma samples using the single-cell-derived subtype signatures. Among these, the Int-Wnt subtype was the most abundant, followed by Int-Hypoxia and PB-KRAS, whereas the Cycling subtype was relatively rare across samples (Fig. 4 a and Table S3 ). Regarding tumor stage, the Int-Hypoxia subtype was found to be more prevalent in Stage I tumors compared to Stage II (Padj = 0.045; Fig. S3 d). Next, we examined the prognostic impact of each subtype on OS. Proportions of Int-Wnt subtype was positively correlated with OS ( r  = 0.4, p  = 0.001) (Fig. 4 b), while PB-KRAS subtype abundance was negatively correlated with survival ( r  = −0.34, p  = 0.007) (Fig. 4 c). To determine whether AoV subtypes independently contribute to prognosis, we performed multivariate Cox regression analyses incorporating clinical covariates. Notably, PB-KRAS subtype was significantly associated with worse OS (hazard ratio; HR = 116.6, 95% confidence interval; CI = 5.4–2496.6, p  = 0.002) and DFS (HR = 101.1, 95% CI = 3.3–3132.4, p  = 0.008), independent of other factors (Fig. 4 e–f), while Int-Wnt subtype was significantly associated with improved prognosis (DFS: HR = 0.1, 95% CI = 0.004–0.7, p  = 0.028) (Fig. 4 f). Consistently, univariate Cox regression analyses supported the prognostic significance of PB-KRAS subtype for both OS and DFS (Fig. S3 e-f). Together, these findings highlight that the composition of epithelial subtypes, particularly PB-KRAS and Int-Wnt subtype, has significant prognostic and clinical relevance in AoV carcinoma. The PB-KRAS subtype is associated with a most distinctly aggressive phenotype and a higher likelihood of recurrence. At the single-cell level, the proportion of Tc- GZMK cells was strongly correlated with the abundance of PB-KRAS subtype within each tumor ( r  = 0.98, p  < 0.001; Fig. 5 c). These Tc- GZMK cells represent a pre-dysfunctional state of CD8 + T cells [ 31 ], characterized by the robust expression of effector molecules such as GZMK and the absence of terminal exhaustion markers like HAVCR2 , while exhibiting moderate levels of early activation markers such as LAG3 (Fig. S4 a). This association was further validated in bulk RNA-seq data, where higher PB-KRAS subtype proportions were positively correlated with Tc- GZMK proportions across patients ( r  = 0.26, p  = 0.037; Fig. 5 d). These results suggest a potential interaction between PB-KRAS subtype and Tc- GZMK cells. We also examined whether their abundance was associated with clinical outcomes. Patients with high Tc- GZMK cell proportions exhibited significantly worse OS compared to those with lower levels (Fig. 5 e). We next explored potential epithelial-immune crosstalk using ligand-receptor interaction analysis. PB-KRAS subtype exhibited enriched interactions with Tc- GZMK cells through multiple ligand-receptor axes, including TGFB2 , SPP1 , and FGF2 , which are well-known mediators of immunosuppressive signaling (Fig. S4 b). These factors are associated with T cell exhaustion, suppression of cytotoxic responses, and immune evasion, suggesting that PB-KRAS subtype may contribute to shaping a dysfunctional yet Tc- GZMK -rich immune microenvironment. Spatial profiling reveals an immunosuppressive microenvironment in PB-KRAS subtype regions To investigate the spatial relationships between cellular subtypes and the tumor microenvironment, we performed Xenium in situ analysis on two representative AoV carcinoma samples, categorized as intestinal type and pancreatobiliary type based on the consensus judgment of experienced pathologists examining the tumor sections (Fig. 5 f). We first used single-cell RNA sequencing to estimate the major cell types and then mapped their spatial distribution across the tissue (Fig. 5 g). To investigate subtype-specific spatial patterns, we next identified and distinguished specific regions within the tumors, focusing on the AoV-ST1 sample, which are characterized by high proportions of Int-Hypoxia, and the AoV-ST2 sample, which are characterized by high proportions of the PB-KRAS subtype (Fig. 5 h). Importantly, the classification of regions derived from scRNA-seq mapping into Int-Hypoxia high (AoV-ST1) and PB-KRAS high (AoV-ST2) categories showed strong agreement with the initial pathological classification. Visualization of the spatial maps revealed a striking co-localization between the PB-KRAS subtype and Tc-GZMK cells (indicated by triangle-shaped dots), with a denser infiltration observed in the PB-KRAS high sample (Fig. 5 h). Quantitative analysis confirmed this observation: the PB-KRAS high sample exhibited a markedly higher proportion of PB-KRAS cells (among all epithelial cells) and a corresponding elevation in the proportion of Tc- GZMK cells (among all T cells) compared to the Int-Hypoxia high sample (Fig. 5 i). To further validate the spatial association between these populations, we performed a nearest neighbor distance analysis using the Xenium spatial coordinates. Our results revealed that Tc- GZMK cells were located significantly closer to PB-KRAS cells, with a mean minimum distance of 114.3 µm, whereas the distance to Int-hypoxia cells was nearly three-fold higher at 321.4 µm (Fig. 5 j). To visually confirm the presence of the Tc- GZMK population, we performed multiplex immunofluorescence using MACSima Imaging System ( n  = 3 per each group; see supplementary methods). Although this population was relatively sparse, pancreatobiliary subtype enriched samples showed higher infiltration of Tc- GZMK cells, whereas intestinal subtype dominant tumors displayed sparse Tc- GZMK infiltration (Fig. S5 a-b). Quantification confirmed that the proportion of Tc- GZMK cells was significantly higher in Pancreatobiliary subtype compared to intestinal subtype tumors ( p  = 0.0375; Fig. S5 c). These initial findings collectively suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype is associated with a distinctive and highly infiltrated tumor microenvironment. PB-KRAS subtype associates with an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment To gain deeper insights into the immune microenvironment of AoV carcinoma, we conducted detailed subclustering analyses specifically focusing on myeloid and B lineage cells. This allowed us to resolve cellular heterogeneity within these immune compartments. Myeloid cells were classified into distinct subpopulations including macrophages, monocytes, dendritic cells (DCs), and mast cells based on canonical lineage markers and differentially expressed genes (Fig. 6 a), with neutrophils excluded from this analysis because they were predominantly derived from a single sample (Fig. S6 a-b). Similarly, B lineage cells were divided into naive B cells and multiple subsets of plasma cells, each characterized by unique transcriptomic signatures (Fig. 6 b). These refined annotations enabled a more precise characterization of cell-type-specific contributions to the tumor microenvironment. Notably, the PB-KRAS subtype exhibited strong positive correlations with macrophage- SPP1 and Tc- GZMK clusters (Fig. 6 c). SPP1 -expressing macrophages have previously been associated with immunosuppressive and pro-tumorigenic functions [ 32 , 33 ]. In addition to the T cell infiltration, the spatial distribution of pro-tumorigenic myeloid cells also exhibited a marked preference for the PB-KRAS-rich environment. The nearest neighbor distance analysis demonstrated that macrophage- SPP1 were predominantly localized in close proximity to the PB-KRAS subtype, with a mean distance of 352.6 µm, compared to a significantly larger distance of 903.0 µm from the Int-hypoxia subtype (Fig. 5 j). To investigate the molecular mechanisms that may underlie this observation, we conducted a formal cell-cell communication analysis between epithelial subtypes and myeloid subclusters. This analysis identified several significant signaling axes, including PTN-ALK, FGF2–FGFR1, and FGF19–FGFR1, which were specifically enriched in the interaction between the PB-KRAS subtype and SPP1 + macrophages (Fig. S6 c). Notably, FGF2 is a well-established mediator known to promote the polarization of tumor-associated macrophages toward a pro-tumorigenic, M2-like state within the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment [ 34 ]. These findings provide molecular evidence that the PB-KRAS subtype actively modulates the functional phenotype of the myeloid compartment, offering a mechanistic basis that extends beyond mere numerical correlation. These findings suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype may develop within, or contribute to, a uniquely immunologically conditioned microenvironment enriched in tumor-promoting macrophages and pre-dysfunctional CD8 + T cells. This immune landscape may underlie the aggressive behavior and recurrence-prone nature of this epithelial subtype. Further mechanistic studies are warranted to clarify the functional significance of these immune–epithelial interactions and evaluate their potential as therapeutic targets. Discussion This study presents the first single-cell transcriptomic analysis of AoV carcinoma, offering a high-resolution landscape of its epithelial and immune cell composition. Previous genomic investigations, primarily based on whole-exome sequencing, have significantly advanced our understanding of AoV carcinoma by identifying recurrent alterations such as ELF3 mutations and WNT pathway dysregulation [ 4 , 5 ]. However, these bulk approaches lack the granularity required to resolve cell type-specific programs and microenvironmental interactions. Our single-cell approach addresses these limitations and provides novel insights into epithelial heterogeneity, differentiation states, and tumor-immune crosstalk in AoV carcinoma. Among the four molecular subtypes identified, our data demonstrate that the intestinal subtype itself is not homogeneous but comprises at least two molecularly distinct programs: one characterized by active WNT/β-catenin signaling (Int-Wnt) and another driven by hypoxia-associated pathways (Int-Hypoxia). The Int-Wnt subtype was defined by robust expression of WNT target genes and selective activation of the MSX1 regulon. MSX1 is known to function downstream of WNT/β-catenin signaling, playing a key role in promoting intestinal tumorigenesis. Its loss suppresses ectopic crypt formation in Apc-deficient models, suggesting that MSX1 is a critical mediator of WNT-driven epithelial transformation [ 26 ]. These features suggest that the Int-Wnt subtype retains a proliferative, WNT-responsive phenotype reminiscent of early intestinal neoplasia. In contrast, the Int-Hypoxia subtype displayed prominent enrichment of hypoxia-related gene sets and strong activation of the SIRT6 regulon. This suggests a mechanism involving SIRT6-enhanced stability of HIF-1α, which is known to promote the expression of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-related transcription factors like SNAIL and TWIST [ 28 ]. The resultant overexpression of SNAIL and TWIST leads to suppression of E-cadherin and induction of Vimentin, hallmark events of EMT [ 28 ]. This molecular cascade facilitates increased cellular plasticity and motility, thereby promoting invasive behavior. EMT has been associated with enhanced metastatic potential and poor recurrence-free survival in several cancers, including papillary thyroid carcinoma, and may similarly portend aggressive clinical behavior in the Int-Hypoxia subtype of AoV carcinoma. By uncovering both a WNT-driven and a hypoxia-induced EMT program within the intestinal group, our analysis emphasizes the subtype’s underlying complexity and suggests that these distinctions may carry prognostic or therapeutic significance. The PB-KRAS subtype emerged as a particularly notable finding in our comprehensive epithelial subtyping. This subtype is defined by elevated KRAS expression and a transcriptional program robustly enriched for KRAS signaling. The PB-KRAS subtype exhibited a pronounced degree of genomic instability, carrying the highest CNV burden among all identified epithelial subtypes. Reflecting these substantial genomic aberrations, which are often associated with aggressive and self-renewal-enhancing phenotypes, we were guided to investigate its developmental hierarchy and specifically focused on evaluating its stem-like properties. Strikingly, the PB-KRAS subtype paradoxically exhibited high developmental potential and stemness scores, comparable to the canonical progenitor-like Cycling subtype. This unique combination of an apparent differentiated PB lineage state possessing high developmental potential defines a non-canonical stem-like epithelial state. Unlike the Cycling subtype, which represents a classical progenitor state, PB-KRAS cells achieve stemness through oncogenic signaling. Specifically, we found that the stemness signature was driven by the transcriptional upregulation of KRAS expression, independent of differential CNV at the KRAS locus. This suggests that elevated KRAS expression forces an aberrant, de-differentiated potential within a seemingly mature lineage. This is consistent with prior findings implicating KRAS signaling in the maintenance of stem-like features in pancreatic cancer cells [ 30 ]. Supporting this stem-like phenotype, HNF1B regulon activity was also selectively enriched in the PB-KRAS subtype. As HNF1B overexpression has been shown to enhance the expression of liver progenitor cell markers and stemness in liver cancer cells [ 27 ], this activation suggests a conserved role in supporting KRAS-associated epithelial states. Clinically, the PB-KRAS subtype was associated with significantly worse OS and DFS, as well as a higher incidence of recurrence. These findings collectively suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype program, defined by unique genomic instability and a KRAS-driven non-canonical stemness, represents the most clinically aggressive AoV subtype identified in this study, associated with poor outcomes and inherent therapeutic resistance. In addition to epithelial heterogeneity, our analysis revealed striking differences in the immune landscape across subtypes. PB-KRAS subtype were enriched for a distinct immune microenvironment characterized by abundant GZMK + CD8 + T cells (Tc-GZMK cells) and SPP1 + macrophages. GZMK enriched cytotoxic T cells, recently described as pre-dysfunctional T cells, represent an intermediate state preceding terminal T cell exhaustion [ 31 ]. Their accumulation within the PB-KRAS tumor microenvironment, coupled with spatial proximity to tumor epithelium and signaling through immunosuppressive ligand-receptor pairs (such as TGFB2 , FGF2 , and SPP1 ), strongly suggests active immune remodeling by tumor cells. These specific axes are known mediators of immunosuppressive signaling. For instance, TGF-β is known to suppress CD8 + T cell cytotoxicity by repressing a distinct program of cytotoxic gene responses, thereby limiting the antitumor immune response [ 35 ]. Similarly, FGF2 has been implicated in promoting T-cell exhaustion by regulating the expression of SPRY1 in esophageal tumor-infiltrating T cells, further impairing T cell function [ 36 ]. SPP1 directly suppresses CD8 + T cell proliferation and interferon-γ production, contributing to immune evasion by the tumor [ 37 ]. The co-enrichment of SPP1 + macrophages, previously implicated in promoting immune evasion and supporting tumor progression, further supports the presence of an immunosuppressive TME in PB-KRAS subtype. Importantly, high abundance of Tc-GZMK cells was associated with poor clinical outcomes, reinforcing the relevance of the immune milieu in disease progression. Taken together, our findings suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype defines a biologically aggressive, stem-like epithelial population that may either arise within or actively sculpt an immunosuppressive TME enriched for dysfunctional immune cell states. This epithelial-immune crosstalk may contribute to tumor recurrence and resistance to therapy. In contrast, the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtypes are characterized by alternative oncogenic programs and immune environments, with divergent prognostic implications. A key limitation of this study is that the observed association between the PB-KRAS subtype and the immunosuppressive TME is based on correlational multi-omics analysis rather than direct functional validation. It is well established that activating KRAS mutations can actively modulate the immune microenvironment by promoting pro-tumorigenic macrophage polarization, inhibiting T-cell cytotoxicity, and accelerating T-cell exhaustion. Moreover, KRAS-mediated metabolic reprogramming may create a feedback loop where metabolite accumulation induces further genomic instability and mutational burden [ 38 ]. Although our findings regarding the PB-KRAS subtype are highly consistent with these known roles of KRAS signaling, further in vivo studies—such as orthotopic or syngeneic mouse models—and co-culture experiments are necessary to definitively prove the causal role of PB-KRAS cells in shaping this specific immunosuppressive niche. Moreover, while the specific ligand-receptor axes identified in this study, such as TGFB2 and SPP1, represent highly promising therapeutic targets, we acknowledge that their functional significance requires further validation in follow-up translational models utilizing functional blocking with neutralizing antibodies or small molecule inhibitors in patient-derived organoid-immune co-culture systems. These insights have potential therapeutic implications. Targeting the KRAS-HNF1B axis or the immunosuppressive mediators enriched in PB-KRAS subtype may offer novel avenues for treatment. Moreover, immunotherapeutic strategies aiming to restore CD8 + T cell functionality or reprogram tumor-associated macrophages may be particularly effective in this context. Future studies should focus on elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying epithelial-immune interactions in AoV carcinoma and evaluating their druggability in preclinical models. Additionally, although the multivariate analysis yielded an inflated hazard ratio due to complete separation in our small cohort ( n  = 62), Bootstrap validation (1,000 resamples) confirmed the statistical stability and robust prognostic value of the PB-KRAS subtype. Given the limited number of patients included in the single-cell analysis, validation in larger multi-institutional cohorts will be important to further establish the generalizability and potential clinical utility of the PB-KRAS subtype classification. Conclusions Our single-cell atlas of AoV carcinoma reveals profound epithelial and immune heterogeneity and identifies a clinically relevant PB-KRAS subtype defined by KRAS-driven non-canonical stem-like features and an immunosuppressive microenvironment. These findings provide a foundation for precision classification of AoV carcinoma and suggest novel therapeutic vulnerabilities for high-risk patients.
