To provide a stricter clustering benchmark beyond ARI and NMI, the DLPFC comparison was further expanded to six additional metrics: Adjusted mutual information (AMI), homogeneity score (HS), Completeness, V‐measure, Fowlkes–Mallows Index (FMI), and Purity. Among all evaluated methods, STWave ranked first across all eight metrics, including ARI (    0.642  ±  0.089    ), NMI (    0.654  ±  0.045    ), FMI (    0.727  ±  0.085    ), and Purity (    0.810  ±  0.054    ), with the complete metric panel reported in Figure  S29 . These results indicate that the advantage of STWave is not restricted to a single clustering metric.  Building on these benchmark results, we used the same controlled ablation to determine whether the contribution of the wavelet‐transform module extended beyond downstream clustering. In the ablation variant, only the wavelet‐transform module was removed, while the remaining neural‐network architecture and training settings were kept unchanged. On the DLPFC benchmark, STWave outperformed the ablation variant under Mclust clustering, increasing ARI from     0.456  ±  0.080     to     0.593  ±  0.074     and NMI from     0.592  ±  0.055     to     0.658  ±  0.041     across 12 slices and three random trials (Figure  6e , Figure  S28  and Table  S17 ). In the clustering‐agnostic evaluation, STWave showed improved preservation of global distance structure and local neighborhoods in the learned embeddings across the 12 DLPFC slices (Figure  S30c ). In the Xenium human breast cancer regions, STWave generally showed closer agreement with the observed marker expression and lower reconstruction errors across seven region‐of‐interest–marker pairs (Figure  S30a,b ). Collectively, these results indicate that the contribution of the wavelet‐transform module is evident in both the learned embeddings and reconstructed expression and is not limited to improvements in clustering metrics.  To further assess whether performance remains stable when more genes are used, STWave was independently evaluated on the DLPFC dataset with 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000, and 6000 highly variable genes. The ARI and NMI distributions remained broadly comparable across these settings, indicating that STWave remained stable when the input gene set was expanded beyond the 1K‐level targeted panels used by Xenium and CosMx SMI (Figure  S27 ). At the individual‐slice level, we next analyzed slice #151672, which exhibits well‐defined cortical layers and white matter (Figure  6a ). STWave achieved an adjusted rand index (ARI) of 0.796 and a normalized mutual information (NMI) of 0.678, accurately delineating all laminar boundaries in close agreement with manual annotations (Figure  6c  and Tables  S8  and  S9 ). By contrast, baseline methods exhibited distinct topological failure modes. Although BayesSpace achieved a relatively high normalized mutual information (NMI: 0.702), it failed to resolve the biological boundary between Layers 4 and 5 and erroneously subdivided Layer 6 into two domains. Similarly, MuCoST, STAGATE, SEDR, and DeepGFT misclassified Layer 3 by fragmenting it into discontinuous regions. Further validation using UMAP and PAGA analyses confirmed that STWave can capture continuous biological trajectories underlying tissue organization. The learned embeddings distinctly separated layer‐specific spots while preserving smooth transitions that recapitulate the physical continuity of the tissue. In contrast, methods such as conST failed to recover this connectivity or to accurately resolve laminar boundaries. This improved performance is likely attributable to the integration of a discrete wavelet transform with a graph attention autoencoder, which enhances layer‐specific molecular signals while attenuating noise (Figure  6d,f  and Figures  S21  and  S22 ).     3  Conclusion  STWave represents a scalable computational paradigm designed to bridge the gap between the massive data volumes of the     μ  ST     era and constrained hardware resources. As ST technologies advance toward subcellular resolution, the exponential increase in spot numbers poses a substantial memory barrier for existing analytical tools. Our framework addresses this challenge by introducing a unified pipeline tailored for ultra‐large ST datasets. It enables routine analysis of hundreds of thousands of spots on standard computing platforms without compromising biological resolution. By formulating spatial domain identification as a joint problem of computational efficiency and signal enhancement, STWave offers a robust solution for decoding tissue heterogeneity at microscopic scales.  The effectiveness of STWave arises from two core mechanisms that jointly balance scalability and accuracy. First, the partition‐and‐sample strategy addresses the memory bottleneck by enabling patch‐based computation during both training and inference. Second, the integration of a discrete wavelet transform mitigates extreme sparsity and noise characteristic of subcellular‐resolution data. Specifically, approximation coefficients capture global tissue patterns, whereas detail coefficients preserve sharp spatial boundaries. The dual‐domain reconstruction loss further encourages the model to learn representations that are consistent across the wavelet and gene‐expression domains, effectively suppressing technical noise while retaining weak but biologically meaningful signals.  Extensive validation across diverse ST platforms underscores STWave's ability to uncover biologically meaningful patterns that are overlooked by existing approaches. Beyond improvements in standard quantitative metrics, STWave consistently resolved subtle yet clinically relevant structures. For example, in colorectal cancer, it delineated the spatial niche of     S  P  P   1  +      tumor‐associated macrophages and pro‐tumor inflammatory regions enriched for     C  X  C  L  8    . In mouse embryonic development, STWave uniquely identified a dorsal forebrain subregion defined by     F  o  x  g  1    , in close agreement with established histological knowledge. Moreover, STWave outperformed 17 baselines on the Visium DLPFC benchmark, demonstrating superior resolution of fine‐grained cortical layers. These results indicate that the combination of multi‐scale modeling and efficient partitioning enables robust generalization across diverse biological contexts and ST technologies.  Despite these advantages, several limitations suggest directions for future improvement. Fixed‐size patching may disrupt continuous spatial structures at boundaries, which could be alleviated by adaptive or overlapping strategies. To quantify this effect, boundary and interior regions were compared on the Xenium human breast cancer dataset under different boundary ranges. The boundary‐region ARI and NMI remained comparable to the corresponding interior‐region values, suggesting that the patch‐based strategy did not introduce substantial performance degradation at patch boundaries in this dataset (Table  S14 ). In addition, representing gene expression as a 1D sequence does not fully capture gene‐gene regulatory relationships; graph‐based embeddings or order‐invariant transforms may provide more expressive alternatives. Finally, extending STWave from two‐dimensional (2D) sections to three‐dimensional (3D) reconstruction or multi‐modal integration would further enhance its applicability.    4  Experimental Section   4.1  Data Description  We evaluated STWave on a collection of ST datasets spanning multiple technologies and spatial resolutions. The study encompasses five platforms: 10x Genomics Visium HD, 10x Genomics Xenium, NanoString CosMx SMI, BGI Stereo‐seq, and 10x Genomics Visium. Among these, Visium HD achieves near‐cellular resolution with     2  ×  2   μ  m     features across a     6.5   mm  ×  6.5   mm     tissue area, with measurements that can be aggregated into coarser spatial spots ranging from     8     to     16   μ  m    . Xenium is an imaging‐based in situ platform that provides single‐cell to subcellular resolution using ready‐to‐use panels of 5000 genes, with options for small add‐ons or fully custom designs. NanoString CosMx SMI similarly achieves single‐cell to subcellular resolution and supports RNA panels targeting about 6000 genes in both FFPE and fresh‐frozen tissues. Stereo‐seq employs DNA nanoball–patterned arrays on flexible chip formats, enabling spatial binning from subcellular to multicellular scales. In contrast, the Visium platform profiles transcriptomes using 55     μ  m     circular spots across a     6.5   mm  ×  6.5   mm     capture area, providing multicellular resolution with one to ten cells per spot. Collectively, these platforms span spatial resolutions from multicellular to subcellular scales, motivating the development of methods that preserve fine‐grained biological detail while maintaining computational efficiency.  To evaluate the accuracy of spatial domain identification, we benchmarked STWave on a human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) dataset comprising 12 tissue slices from three donors, with each capture area containing about 4000 spots and 33 538 genes. To assess performance at single‐cell and subcellular resolutions, we analyzed a diverse array of high‐resolution ST datasets: a Visium HD human colorectal cancer slice (P2) containing 5 45 913 spots and 18 085 genes; two Xenium datasets, including a human breast cancer dataset featuring 1 67 780 spots across 313 genes and a human kidney cancer dataset containing 56 510 spots across 377 genes; and a CosMx SMI lung cancer dataset consisting of 87 589 spots and 960 genes. The longitudinal Stereo‐seq mouse embryo series (stages E13.5–E16.5) was further utilized, with the E16.5 sample totaling 1 55 741 spots and 28 579 genes. To test high‐resolution scalability under resource‐constrained environments, we generated a series of simulated datasets from the Human Lung Cell Atlas, spanning     5  ×   10  3      to     6.4  ×   10  5      spots. This comprehensive collection covers a continuous spectrum from small‐scale to ultra‐large‐scale data. Collectively, these benchmarks evaluate whether STWave preserves spatial fidelity and maintains manageable resource consumption as data volume increases, while highlighting where baseline methods succumb to oversmoothing of fine structures, boundary fragmentation, or computational failure.    4.2  Data Preprocessing  Gene expression data were processed using Scanpy. For datasets containing at least 3000 genes, highly variable genes were identified from the raw counts using the Seurat v3 method, and the top 3000 highly variable genes were retained. The resulting expression matrix was then normalized on a per‐spot basis and log‐transformed. For datasets with fewer than 3000 genes, all genes were retained before normalization and log transformation, as in the Xenium human breast cancer and CosMx SMI human lung cancer datasets.    4.3  Spatial Neighbor Graph Construction  We construct a spatial graph based on the Euclidean distances between spot coordinates. Spatial relationships are encoded as an undirected    k   ‐nearest‐neighbor graph, denoted      G  spatial   =   (   V  spatial   ,   E  spatial   )     , where     V  spatial     denotes the set of spots and     E  spatial     denotes the set of undirected edges connecting neighboring spots. The adjacency matrix is denoted      A  spatial   ∈    {  0  ,  1  }    n  ×  n      , where    n    is the number of spots. For vertices    i    and    j   , we set      a  spatial   i  j    =  1     if    j    belongs to the set of    k    nearest neighbors of    i   , and      a  spatial   i  j    =  0     otherwise. Each spot is connected to its    k    nearest neighbors, and the resulting graph is treated as undirected. In our experiments, we set     k  =  8     for simulated data, Visium HD, Xenium, and Stereo‐seq datasets, and     k  =  6     for standard 10x Visium datasets.  Based on the constructed spatial graph, STWave prunes edges that are unlikely to convey meaningful local information. We first embed the gene expression matrix using PCA and obtain an initial partition of spots via the Louvain algorithm. Edge pruning is then performed in two stages. In the first stage, edges connecting spots assigned to different clusters are removed to prevent premature information propagation across heterogeneous regions. In the second stage, spurious long‐range connections are eliminated using distance‐based outlier detection with an Isolation Forest [ 46 ]. Specifically, edges with unusually large Euclidean lengths (e.g., exceeding the global mean plus one standard deviation) are flagged and removed. The resulting pruned graph is denoted      G  pruned   =   (   V  pruned   ,   E  pruned   )     .    4.4  Wavelet Representation of Gene Expression  ST data are high‐dimensional and sparse, characterized by pronounced zero inflation, technical noise, multi‐scale texture, and fragile tissue boundaries. These properties often lead to over‐smoothing, attenuation of weak biological signals, and unstable alignment across tissue sections. To disentangle background variation from edge information across multiple scales, we represent the expression profile of each spot as a 1D discrete signal ordered by gene index and apply a 1D discrete wavelet transform [ 47 ]. This 1D representation is used as a computationally efficient multi‐scale feature transform rather than as an explicit model of gene regulatory interactions. To assess whether the imposed gene order affects downstream performance, randomized gene‐order experiments were conducted on the DLPFC dataset, where ARI and NMI remained stable across five random orders (Figure  S23 ).  Let     X  ∈   R   n  ×  m       denote the gene expression matrix, where    n    is the number of spots and    m    is the number of genes. For each spot‐specific expression vector      x  i   ∈   R  m     , with     i  =  1  ,  …  ,  n    , we initialize      a  0   =   x  i      and apply the discrete wavelet transform as follows:

        d   j  +  1     [  r  ]       =   ∑   k  =  0    N  −  1    g   [  k  −  2  r  ]   ·   a  j    [  k  ]   ,       
 where     a  l     denotes the approximation coefficients at the decomposition level    l   , capturing low‐frequency trends obtained via low‐pass filtering and downsampling.     d  l     denotes the corresponding detail coefficients, representing high‐frequency components extracted through high‐pass filtering and downsampling. The filters    h    and    g    correspond to low‐pass and high‐pass kernels, respectively. The index    k    denotes the convolution offset,    N    is the length of the input signal at the current level, and    r    indexes the resulting output coefficients. After    j    levels of wavelet decomposition, each expression vector is represented by a multiscale coefficient set     (   a  j   ,   d  j   ,  …  ,   d  2   ,   d  1   )    .  We construct a cross‐scale representation by concatenating wavelet coefficients across decomposition levels and frequency bands. Specifically,

 (4)

To further enhance representation learning in the setting of limited computational resources, we construct a masked coefficient matrix     C  mask     as a complementary view to the complete wavelet features. Let      c  i   =   [   a  j   ,   d  j   ,  …  ,   d  1   ]   ∈   R   d  wc       denote the wavelet coefficient vector for spot    i   . A binary mask     m  ∈    {  0  ,  1  }    d  wc       is applied to retain approximation coefficients (    a  j    ) while suppressing high‐frequency detail components, yielding
 
 (5)

Stacking these vectors forms      C  mask   ∈   R   n  ×   d  wc       , which emphasizes low‐frequency global expression patterns and reduces sensitivity to technical noise.    4.5  Subgraph Partitioning and Sampling  To ensure the scalability of STWave while minimizing GPU and CPU overhead, we implement a partition‐and‐sample subgraph strategy. The global ST dataset is first decomposed into spatially contiguous patches based on coordinates, with the original spot indices preserved to maintain data integrity. The granularity of this partitioning is governed by a tunable hyperparameter,    m   , which represents the number of patches along each dimension. To optimize the trade‐off between computational efficiency and neighborhood preservation, we recommend an     m  ×  m     grid configuration where     m  =  round     n  /  10  ,  000        (Table  S7 ). This heuristic ensures that each patch contains approximately 10 000 spots on average, preventing the loss of local structural information associated with overly fine partitioning while avoiding the prohibitive memory demands of excessively large patches. Leveraging the stored indices, we utilize the PyTorch Geometric (PyG) framework to sample subgraphs from both the initial spatial graph     G  spatial     and the pruned graph     G  pruned    . This sampling mechanism is designed to preserve internal patch topology and maintain critical boundary connectivity across the spatial domain.    4.6  Graph Attention Autoencoder  Inspired by STAGATE [ 14 ], we employ a four‐layer autoencoder composed of two graph attention blocks and two linear layers to learn graph‐informed embeddings for ST analysis. The encoder consists of two layers. The first layer is a multi‐head graph attention layer that aggregates features from local neighborhoods, while the second layer applies a linear projection to generate low‐dimensional spot embeddings. We denote      H  0   =  C  ∈   R   n  ×   d  wc        as the input feature matrix, where    n    denotes the number of spots and     d  wc     is the dimension of the wavelet coefficient representation. The adjacency matrix     A  ∈   R   n  ×  n       defines candidate spatial neighbors, and     S  i     denotes the neighborhood of spot    i   , including the spot itself. The first graph attention layer is defined as
 
 (6)

Non‐linear transformations are governed by activation functions     σ  1     and     σ  2    , which ensure the model captures complex spatial dependencies. Propagating the first‐layer representation     H  1     through graph convolution under each adjacency yields two intermediate feature matrices,     H  spatial  1     and     H  pruned  1    . Taking     H  2     as input, it first applies a graph attention–based aggregation to propagate neighborhood information, followed by a linear projection that maps the features back to wavelet coefficient space:

The final reconstruction is      C  ^   =   H  4   ∈   R   n  ×   d  wc       . This design couples attention‐driven neighborhood aggregation with linear projection to achieve graph‐informed reconstruction.    4.7  Inverse Wavelet Transform  To more accurately recover spot‐level gene expression patterns, we apply the inverse discrete wavelet transform (IDWT) to both the reconstructed coefficient matrix     C  ^     and masked coefficient matrix     C  mask    . Specifically, we reverse the concatenation defined in Equations ( 3 ) and ( 4 ) to recover scale‐specific wavelet components. For each spot    i    (    i  =  1  ,  …  ,  n    ), a split operator maps the reconstructed coefficient vector      c  ^   i     to the set     (   a  J   ,   d  J   ,  …  ,   d  1   )    , where    J    denotes the number of wavelet decomposition levels.  We then perform the IDWT to recover the signal. The single‐level reconstruction is

Iteratively applying Equation ( 11 ) from level    J    down to level     1     yields the reconstructed gene expression vector       x  ^   i   ∈   R  m      for spot    i   .  Stacking the reconstructed vectors      x  ^   i     across all spots yields the reconstructed expression matrix       X  ^   wc   ∈   R   n  ×  m      . Applying the same inverse discrete wavelet transform to the masked coefficient matrix     C  mask     produces      X  ^   mask    , which preserves low‐frequency approximation components while suppressing high‐frequency noise. Together, the pair     (    X  ^   wc   ,    X  ^   mask   )     provides complementary reconstructions that support robust downstream analysis.    4.8  Attention Fusion Mechanism  We integrate      X  ^   wc     and      X  ^   mask     using an attention‐based fusion module. The reconstruction      X  ^   wc     retains high‐frequency details but exhibits attenuated low‐frequency structure, while      X  ^   mask     preserves global low‐frequency trends while discarding fine‐scale variations. To balance these complementary properties, we employ spot‐level or gene‐level attention to adaptively weight the two reconstructions, yielding a more accurate and biologically faithful expression profile. Formally,
 
 (12) 
       γ  m      =    exp     a  m  ⊤    [     X  ^   wc   ∥    X  ^   mask    ]       ∑   j  =  1   2   exp     a  j  ⊤    [     X  ^   wc   ∥    X  ^   mask    ]      ,   m  ∈   {  1  ,  2  }   ,       
 
 
 (13) 
       X  ^      =   γ  1   ⊙    X  ^   wc    +    γ  2   ⊙    X  ^   mask   ,       
 where     γ  m     denotes the learned attention coefficient, and the vectors     a  m     are trainable parameters, while    ⊙    represents element‐wise multiplication. This fusion mechanism enables complementary integration of low‐frequency structural information and high‐frequency detailed signals.    4.9  Loss Function  The objective function of STWave is formulated as a dual‐term loss that jointly optimizes reconstruction fidelity in both the wavelet and gene‐expression domains. The first term measures the reconstruction error of wavelet coefficients, preserving essential multiscale structural features, while the second term enforces accurate recovery of gene expression in the original space. The overall loss    L    is defined as
 
 (14) 
    min  L  =  α   1  n    ∑   i  =  1   n    ∥    C  i   −    C  ^   i    ∥  +    1  n    ∑   i  =  1   n    ∥   X  i   −    X  ^   i   ∥   ,    
 where     C  i     and      C  ^   i     denote the original and reconstructed wavelet representations for spot    i   , respectively;     X  i     and      X  ^   i     are the corresponding original and reconstructed gene expression vectors;    n    is the total number of spots; and    α    is a tunable hyperparameter controlling the contribution of the wavelet‐domain reconstruction term.    4.10  Training and Inference  After partitioning the original tissue slice into spatial patches, we randomize the patch order and train the model iteratively on each patch. As described above, the spot‐level expression vector is treated as a 1D discrete signal and transformed via a 1D discrete wavelet transform to obtain multiscale coefficients. These coefficients are processed by the autoencoder to generate reconstructed wavelet representations. The inverse discrete wavelet transform is then applied to map the reconstructed coefficients back to gene expression space, yielding a patch‐level reconstructed profile. In parallel, detail coefficients are masked and passed through the same inverse transform to produce a complementary reconstruction emphasizing low‐frequency structure. An attention‐based fusion module adaptively integrates the two reconstructions. Model training is guided by the loss function in Equation ( 14 ) and proceeds for a predefined number of epochs.  After training, inference is performed at the patch level to minimize GPU and CPU memory usage. Using the stored spot index sets, patch‐wise predictions are mapped back to their original spatial coordinates on the full tissue slice. This design substantially reduces computational overhead while preserving reconstruction fidelity (Figure  2a  and Figure  S1 ). The reconstructed expression profiles, together with the learned graph‐informed embeddings, are subsequently used for downstream tasks such as clustering, visualization, and spatial analysis.    4.11  Spatial Clustering  Following the above procedure, each spot is represented by a graph‐informed embedding and a reconstructed gene expression profile. We use the learned embeddings for spatial domain identification with standard clustering algorithms, including Mclust [ 48 ], Louvain [ 9 ], and Leiden [ 41 ]. For tissue slices with manual annotations, we apply Mclust and set the number of clusters to match the annotated domains. When annotations are unavailable or when latent spatial structure is to be discovered, we employ Louvain or Leiden clustering with an appropriately selected resolution. To ensure fair evaluation on annotated benchmarks, we follow the recommended settings for each method and tune the resolution parameters such that the inferred number of domains equals the annotation count, enabling balanced comparisons across methods.    4.12  Parameter Sensitivity Analysis  To evaluate the impact of the dual‐domain reconstruction loss weight    α    (defined in Equation ( 14 )) on model performance, we conducted a sensitivity analysis on the     12     human DLPFC slices. We varied the hyperparameter    α    from     5     to     30     in increments of     5     to assess its impact on clustering performance. As summarized in Tables  S10  and  S11 , STWave exhibits a clear performance trend, achieving optimal results at     α  =  20    . At this setting, the model attains the highest clustering accuracy, with a mean ARI of     0.642     and a mean NMI of     0.654    .  Further analysis of mean and variance across different    α    underscores the robustness of STWave. Although performance peaks at     α  =  20    , clustering accuracy remains stable throughout the evaluated range, indicating limited sensitivity to moderate hyperparameter variations. Notably, at     α  =  20    , the standard deviation of NMI is minimized (    0.045    ), while the standard deviation of ARI remains low (    0.089    ). This consistently low variance across 12 tissue slices suggests that a fixed setting of     α  =  20     generalizes well across samples without requiring slice‐specific tuning. To further assess whether this setting transfers beyond DLPFC, the same sensitivity analysis was performed on the Xenium human breast cancer dataset and the mouse embryo dataset using three independent random seeds. On the Xenium dataset,     α  =  20     achieved the highest ARI (    0.441  ±  0.026    ) and a comparable NMI (    0.549  ±  0.001    ) across the tested range. On the mouse embryo dataset,     α  =  20     achieved the highest ARI (    0.415  ±  0.018    ) and NMI (    0.612  ±  0.001    ) (Tables  S12  and  S13 ). These results demonstrate that STWave exhibits a stable optimization landscape and strong generalization performance.     Conflicts of Interest  The authors declare no conflicts of interest. title: Cell-resolved spatial mapping of antibody-drug conjugate targets in breast cancer.
xenium_reason: Xenium is explicitly used for validation
evidence_text:
Cell-resolved spatial mapping of antibody-drug conjugate targets in breast cancer.

Background

Antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) activity and target-dependent on-target/off-tumor toxicity depends in part on which cells express the target antigen, a feature that bulk assays cannot resolve.

Methods

We analyzed a publicly available whole-transcriptome CosMx breast tumor dataset including 154,816 cells and 18,934 genes. Eleven clinically relevant ADC targets were profiled across seven annotated lineages. Findings were contextualized using TCGA-BRCA bulk transcriptomes (1,097 tumors and 114 normal tissues) and assessed in two public Xenium breast cancer specimens.

Results

HER2 (ERBB2), TROP2 (TACSTD2), HER3 (ERBB3), NECTIN4 and MUC1 were enriched in tumor epithelium. B7-H3 (CD276) was highest in endothelial and myoepithelial cells, with similar mean expression in stromal and tumor cells. PSMA (FOLH1) was enriched in endothelium. TCGA-BRCA tumor-normal differences did not identify these cellular sources. No overall-survival association remained after multiple-testing correction or covariate adjustment. HER2 and TROP2 tumor enrichment recurred in both Xenium specimens, whereas EGFR was not tumor restricted.

Conclusions

Cell-resolved spatial profiling separated ADC targets enriched in tumor epithelium from those expressed in vascular and stromal compartments. B7-H3 and PSMA localization was consistent with prior immunohistochemical reports and is confirmatory. These RNA-level results do not establish surface-protein abundance, ADC response, or clinical toxicity. Low-abundance microenvironmental findings remain based on a single discovery specimen and require protein-level validation. Protein-level confirmation, and correlation with ADC efficacy and toxicity, are required before these maps can inform clinical decisions. Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) link a target-specific antibody to a cytotoxic payload and are now central to breast-cancer treatment [ 2 ]. Trastuzumab emtansine established the class in HER2-positive disease [ 3 ], extending median progression-free survival from 6.4 to 9.6 months and median overall survival from 25.1 to 30.9 months relative to lapatinib plus capecitabine. Trastuzumab deruxtecan and the TROP2-directed agents Sacituzumab govitecan and datopotamab deruxtecan have since broadened their use across breast cancer subtypes [ [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. In the long-term DESTINY-Breast04 analysis, investigator-assessed median progression-free survival was 8.8 versus 4.2 months (hazard ratio, 0.36), and median overall survival was 22.9 versus 16.8 months (hazard ratio, 0.69), with trastuzumab deruxtecan versus treatment of the physician's choice in HER2-low advanced breast cancer [ 4 ]. In the final ASCENT analysis, Sacituzumab govitecan improved median progression-free survival to 4.8 versus 1.7 months (hazard ratio 0.41) and median overall survival to 11.8 versus 6.9 months (hazard ratio 0.51) in metastatic triple-negative breast cancer [ 5 ]. HER3, NECTIN4 , folate receptor-α, B7-H3, MUC1 and CEACAM5 are among the additional targets in clinical development [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]; the molecular alterations of MUC1 and their therapeutic exploitation have been reviewed recently [ 11 ]. For an ADC, tissue-level abundance is not enough. The target must also be located on the relevant cells. Expression in stroma, vasculature or normal epithelium can contribute to target-dependent on-target/off-tumor toxicity, but ADC toxicity is multifactorial and also reflects payload cytotoxicity, platform-related properties, and host factors [ 12 ]. The clinical burden can nonetheless be substantial. In the updated DESTINY-Breast04 analysis, adjudicated drug-related interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis occurred in 12.1% of patients receiving trastuzumab deruxtecan, including 1.1% grade 5 events [ 4 ]. In the final ASCENT analysis, the most common grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events with Sacituzumab govitecan included neutropenia (52%) and diarrhea (12%) [ 5 ]. Conversely, target-negative tumor cells may escape direct binding, although a membrane-permeable payload can affect neighboring cells through a bystander effect [ 13 ]. Bulk assays and tissue-averaged immunohistochemistry do not resolve the cellular source of a target signal. The broader importance of tissue architecture extends beyond ADCs to other tumor-directed delivery platforms, including nanocarriers influenced by vascular permeability and retention, as well as stimuli-responsive nanoparticles under development for breast cancer [ 14 , 15 ]. Cell-resolved target assessment is already used in the chimeric antigen receptor T-cell field to anticipate on-target/off-tumor effects [ 16 ]. For ADCs, bulk surveys have catalogued target expression across tumors and normal tissues, including a 54-target pan-cancer analysis [ 17 ]. A post-mortem breast cancer series also compared metastases with matched normal organs [ 18 ]. In high-grade serous ovarian cancer, dissociated single-cell RNA sequencing identified clinical ADC targets that were most often restricted to cancer cells [ 19 ]. Spatial profiling has therefore been proposed as a means of interpreting target availability in tissue context [ 20 ]. Breast single-cell atlases have examined heterogeneity in ERBB2 and TACSTD2, but primarily within the malignant epithelial compartment [ 21 ]. Few studies have spatially identified multiple ADC targets across malignant and non-malignant compartments in breast cancer. Imaging-based transcriptomics can provide this information while preserving histological structure [ [22] , [23] , [24] , [25] ]. We therefore mapped 11 ADC targets in a publicly available whole-transcriptome breast cancer specimen, examined the recurrence of selected patterns in two public Xenium specimens, and compared the findings with TCGA-BRCA bulk transcriptomes. The study is descriptive. Its purpose is to identify which cells contribute to each target transcript and to show where tissue-level abundance may obscure that source. Materials and methods Single-cell spatial dataset We used the public CosMx Spatial Molecular Imager Human Whole Transcriptome FFPE breast dataset (Bruker Spatial Biology, "breast discovery" release, sample S0) [ 22 ]. The dataset contains one tumor specimen, which served as the discovery sample. Selected findings were examined in two additional public Xenium specimens (the cross-specimen Xenium analysis). We obtained the cell-by-gene matrix, cell metadata, and cell polygons from the public repository. The complete dataset contained approximately 645,000 cells. To make the analysis tractable using standard hardware, we drew a reproducible random subsample (seed = 1) and retained cells with at least 50 detected RNA molecules. This yielded 154,816 cells. Removing negative-control and system-control probes left 18,934 genes. Global coordinates were converted from pixels to micrometers using a scale of 0.12028 µm per pixel. We also split the retained cells into two random halves and compared cell-type mean target-expression matrices to assess sensitivity to subsampling. Clustering, annotation and differential expression Analyses were performed in R 4.5.2 with Seurat 5.5.1 [ 26 ]. Counts were log-normalized to counts per 10,000, then subjected to a natural-log transformation. We scaled the 2,000 most variable genes and used 30 principal components to construct a shared-nearest-neighbor graph. Louvain clustering was run at resolution 0.5, followed by UMAP embedding. Clusters were assigned to seven lineages using module scores for canonical markers and established breast cell-type signatures [ 27 ]. The lineages were tumor epithelial, fibroblast/stromal, myeloid, B/plasma, T, myoepithelial, and endothelial. One-versus-rest Wilcoxon rank-sum tests identified positive cell-type markers, with at least 10% detection, a minimum log2 fold-change of 0.25, and at most 500 cells per group. P values were adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg method. These cell-level tests treat cells from one specimen as independent observations. We therefore used them to describe within-sample marker specificity and placed greater weight on effect sizes than on nominal P values. ADC-target analysis We examined eleven clinically relevant ADC targets: ERBB2 (HER2), TACSTD2 (TROP2), ERBB3 (HER3), NECTIN4, FOLR1 (FRα), CEACAM5 (CEA), CD276 (B7-H3), MUC1, MET, EGFR and FOLH1 (PSMA). For each cell type, we calculated mean log-normalized expression and the number and fraction of cells with detectable expression. Per-cell expression was also mapped in tissue coordinates. Cross-platform single-target detection comparison To describe cross-platform differences in single-target detection, we compared ERBB2 and TACSTD2 between the whole-transcriptome CosMx dataset and a 313-gene Xenium breast panel [ 23 ]. For each dataset, we calculated the fraction of tumor cells with zero counts for the target gene. The assays were applied to different specimens and used different chemistries and panel sizes; this descriptive comparison was not designed to isolate a platform or panel-design effect. Receptor subtype, spillover control and spatial organization For each target, we report the number and fraction of expressing cells, along with the mean expression. This provides cellular support for findings in low-abundance microenvironments. To assess whether FOLH1 and CD276 enrichment could reflect transcript spillover across cell boundaries, we built a k-nearest-neighbor graph (k = 10) from cell centroids. We calculated the proportion of tumor-epithelial neighbors for each cell, then compared expression in the enriched lineage between cells with few (<25%) and many (>50%) tumor neighbors. The receptor phenotype was inferred from tumor-cell expression of ESR1, PGR, and ERBB2 , with GATA3 and MKI67 as context. This RNA-based classification is not equivalent to immunohistochemical receptor status. Cell-type neighborhood enrichment followed the approach implemented in Squidpy [ 28 ]. For each ordered cell-type pair, we compared the observed number of graph edges with a null distribution from 100 permutations of cell-type labels and expressed the result as a z-score. Bulk transcriptomic contextualization (TCGA-BRCA) TCGA-BRCA gene-level expression (log2(normalized count + 1)) and clinical data were obtained from the UCSC Xena TCGA hub [ 29 , 30 ]. Sample barcodes identified 1,097 primary tumors and 114 solid-tissue normals. In this dataset, NECTIN4 is recorded under its alias PVRL4 and was mapped accordingly. Tumor-versus-normal differences were tested for each target by the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment. Overall survival was derived from vital status and time to death or last follow-up. The full survival cohort contained 1,080 patients. For each target, we fitted a univariable Cox model using continuous expression and performed a median-split log-rank test. We interpreted these P values in the context of the 11 tested targets and did not search for additional endpoints and subgroups. Multivariable Cox models were fitted separately in the 808 patients with complete data for age, pathologic stage, and PAM50 intrinsic subtype. Cross-specimen validation on Xenium We analyzed two additional public Xenium breast cancer specimens: the Human Breast invasive ductal carcinoma sample and the breast cancer reference block [ 23 ]. The invasive ductal carcinoma specimen came from a different patient. Public metadata did not establish patient-level independence of the reference block. We used the vendor-supplied graph-based clusters and assigned cells to the same lineages by marker scores. Four ADC targets were represented in the Xenium panel: ERBB2, TACSTD2, MUC1, and EGFR . For each target, we compared detection fractions between tumor epithelial and non-tumor cells. Detection fraction was chosen because absolute expression is not directly comparable across platforms with different panel sizes and sequencing depths. Results A seven-lineage single-cell spatial map of the breast tumor Unsupervised clustering produced 15 clusters, which were assigned to seven cell types ( Fig. 1 ). Tumor epithelium was the largest compartment (95,803 cells; 61.9%). Fibroblast/stromal and myeloid cells each accounted for 10.3%, followed by B/plasma cells (6.9%), T cells (5.3%), myoepithelial cells (2.7%), and endothelial cells (2.6%). Quality-control distributions are shown in Supplementary Fig. S2. These populations occupied coherent tissue regions, with tumor epithelium forming contiguous fields and glandular structures ( Fig. 1 B). One-versus-rest testing identified 4,449 positive markers. The leading markers matched the assigned lineages, including PIP, SERHL2, and MLPH in the tumor epithelium; COL1A1, LUM, and POSTN in the stroma; and EGFL7, PLVAP, and FLT1 in the endothelium ( Fig. 2 ; Supplementary Table S4). The same correspondence was seen for myeloid ( APOE, LYZ, C1QC ), B/plasma ( IGKC, IGHA1, JCHAIN ), T ( GNLY, GZMA, ITGAE ) and myoepithelial cells ( ACTA2, MCAM, CSPG4 ). Fig. 1 Single-cell spatial map of the breast tumor. (A) Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) of 154,816 analyzed cells from one CosMx breast tumor specimen, colored by seven annotated cell types. (B) Spatial distribution of the same cells using tissue coordinates in micrometers. Each point represents a cell centroid. The same cell-type color key is used in both panels. Fig. 2 Cell-type marker expression in the discovery specimen. The five positive one-versus-rest markers with the largest average log2 fold change are shown for each of seven cell types. Dot color represents mean log-normalized expression across all cells in the indicated lineage, including zero-count cells. Dot size represents the fraction of cells with a nonzero gene count. The size-key values are fractions: 0.25, 0.50 and 0.75 correspond to 25%, 50% and 75%, respectively. Expression was normalized to 10,000 counts per cell and transformed using ln(1 + x). Marker-test results are provided in Supplementary Table S4. ADC targets show tumor-enriched and microenvironment-enriched patterns The eleven ADC targets followed two broad patterns ( Fig. 3 ). MUC1 (mean log-normalized expression 0.82), HER2/ ERBB2 (0.68), NECTIN4 (0.60), TROP2/ TACSTD2 (0.52) and HER3/ ERBB3 (0.39) were highest in tumor epithelium. Their mean expression in non-malignant compartments was 0.14 or lower. Spatial maps showed that HER2 and TROP2 expression were associated with the tumor-epithelial regions of the section ( Fig. 4 ). Fig. 3 ADC-target expression across cell types. Dot plot of 11 antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) targets in the CosMx discovery specimen. Dot color represents mean log-normalized expression across all cells in each lineage, including zero-count cells. Dot size represents the fraction of cells with a nonzero gene count; size-key values of 0.1-0.4 correspond to 10%-40%. Expression was normalized to 10,000 counts per cell and transformed using ln(1 + x). MUC1, HER2, NECTIN4, TROP2 and HER3 had their highest mean expression in tumor epithelium. B7-H3 was highest in endothelial and myoepithelial cells, and PSMA was highest in endothelium. Cell counts and detection fractions are provided in Supplementary Table S1. These measurements concern RNA expression. Fig. 4 Spatial expression of representative ADC targets. Per-cell expression of HER2 (ERBB2, upper left), TROP2 (TACSTD2, upper right), PSMA (FOLH1, lower left) and B7-H3 (CD276, lower right) in the CosMx discovery specimen. Each point represents a cell centroid. The four panels use the same tissue coordinates and a common expression color scale. Expression was normalized to 10,000 counts per cell and transformed using ln(1 + x). The maps show transcript localization and do not establish surface-protein abundance. Other targets were expressed preferentially outside the tumor compartment. B7-H3/ CD276 was highest in endothelial (0.35) and myoepithelial cells (0.31), followed by fibroblast/stromal and tumor cells (both 0.16). PSMA/ FOLH1 was concentrated in endothelium (0.47), whereas mean tumor-cell expression was 0.05. This distribution agrees with the reported localization of PSMA to tumor-associated neovasculature rather than breast carcinoma cells [ 31 ]. FOLR1 and CEACAM5 remained low across all cell types in this specimen (≤0.10). The microenvironmental findings were supported by the number of cells expressing (Supplementary Table S1). PSMA was detected in 20.0% of endothelial cells (817 of 4,076) and 3.2% of tumor cells. B7-H3 was detected in 16.0% of endothelial cells, 12.9% of myoepithelial cells, and 9.5% of tumor cells. Low PSMA expression in tumor cells argues against tumor-derived transcript spillover as the main explanation for endothelial enrichment. In the neighborhood analysis, endothelial cells with fewer than 25% tumor neighbors still had a mean PSMA expression of 0.39 (n = 2,282), compared with 0.05 in tumor cells. B7-H3 enrichment in stroma, endothelium and myoepithelium was also retained in cells located away from tumor epithelium (Supplementary Table S2). Single-target detection differed between platforms and specimens In the CosMx whole-transcriptome specimen, 60% of tumor cells had zero ERBB2 counts, and 68% had zero TACSTD2 counts. In the targeted 313-gene Xenium specimen, the corresponding fractions were 3.5% and 11%. Because the assays were applied to different tissue specimens and used different chemistries and panel sizes, these differences cannot be attributed solely to assay design. They nevertheless caution against interpreting a zero count as absence of target expression over spatial transcriptomic platforms. Tumor receptor phenotype and spatial organization Among tumor cells, ERBB2 was the most highly expressed receptor gene (mean 0.68; detected in 36.6% of cells). ESR1 (0.09; 5.8%) and PGR (0.04; 2.7%) were low. This RNA profile is compatible with, but not diagnostic of, a HER2-enriched or hormone-receptor-negative phenotype. The HER2 and TROP2 findings should therefore be interpreted in the context of these receptors. Neighborhood analysis showed strong self-association of the tumor epithelium (z = 507) and negative associations with all non-malignant cell types. The largest negative values were observed in myeloid cells (z = -308) and fibroblast/stromal cells (z = -294). Among non-malignant populations, fibroblasts co-localized most strongly with myeloid cells (z = 131), whereas endothelial cells co-localized most strongly with myoepithelial cells (z = 137; Supplementary Fig. S3). Subsampling had little effect. Two random halves of the retained cells produced nearly identical cell-type mean target-expression matrices (Pearson r = 0.998). HER2 and TROP2 tumor enrichment recurs in additional Xenium specimens Both Xenium specimens were public datasets distinct from the CosMx discovery sample, although only the invasive ductal carcinoma specimen was known to come from a different patient. We therefore assessed cross-specimen recurrence without treating the reference block as a separate patient-level replicate (Supplementary Fig. S4, Supplementary Table S3). Because panel content and sequencing depth differed, the comparison used detection fractions. Ranking cell types by mean expression gave the same ordering. Tumor epithelium had the highest HER2/ ERBB2 and TROP2/ TACSTD2 expression in all six specimen-by-target comparisons. In the invasive ductal carcinoma specimen, for example, TROP2 was detected in 84% of tumor cells and 26% of non-tumor cells. MUC1 showed the same pattern where it was included in the panel. EGFR differed. In both Xenium specimens, EGFR was detected as often as or more often in non-tumor cells, with the highest levels in myoepithelial cells. Bulk tumor-versus-normal expression In TCGA-BRCA (1,097 tumors and 114 normal tissues), six targets were higher in tumor tissue: CEACAM5 (log2 fold-change +4.1), MUC1 (+2.1), CD276 (+0.85), ERBB3 (+0.85), NECTIN4 (+0.75) and ERBB2 (+0.54). All adjusted P values were below 0.001 ( Fig. 5 ; Supplementary Table S5). TACSTD2 did not differ between groups (log2 fold-change -0.29; P = 0.06). Four targets were lower in tumors: FOLR1 (-3.8), EGFR (-3.5), MET (-2.4) and FOLH1 (-1.6). These bulk contrasts are influenced by tissue composition and do not identify the cell type expressing the gene. B7-H3 illustrates the distinction, as it was higher in bulk tumor tissue but arose mainly from endothelial, myoepithelial and stromal cells in the spatial data. Fig. 5 ADC-target expression in TCGA-BRCA tumors and normal tissues. Box plots show log2(normalized count + 1) expression of 11 ADC-target genes in primary tumors (n = 1,097; red) and solid-tissue normal samples (n = 114; blue). The center line is the median, boxes span the 25th-75th percentiles, and whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 times the interquartile range. Points beyond the whiskers are outliers. The y-axis range differs between gene panels. Two-sided Wilcoxon comparisons and Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted P values are reported in Supplementary Table S5. No ADC target shows a strong association with overall survival Among the 1,080 patients with survival data, no univariable association remained significant after correction for eleven targets. The lowest nominal P values in this full cohort were observed for NECTIN4 in the continuous Cox model (P = 0.040) and the median-split log-rank test (P = 0.053; Supplementary Fig. S1; Supplementary Table S6). The complete-covariate subset contained 808 patients. In this subset, CEACAM5 had a nominal univariable association (P = 0.019), which weakened after adjustment for age, pathologic stage, and PAM50 subtype (hazard ratio 1.22; P = 0.071; Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted P = 0.478). No target was associated with overall survival after covariate adjustment (Supplementary Table S7). These analyses do not support a strong single-gene prognostic effect, although the unselected cohort and limited event count constrain the inference. Discussion At the RNA level, the eleven ADC targets separated into two expression patterns in the discovery specimen. HER2, TROP2, HER3, NECTIN4 and MUC1 were concentrated in tumor epithelium. Among these, MUC1 had the highest mean expression, consistent with its long-standing status as a tumor-associated antigen and with continuing efforts to exploit MUC1 alterations therapeutically [ 11 ]. B7-H3 and PSMA were more prominent in stromal or vascular compartments. Bulk and tissue-averaged assays cannot resolve this difference in cellular source. Recovery of the established PSMA neovascular pattern provides an internal check on the cell assignments. These data do not estimate the therapeutic index, which also depends on surface protein abundance, internalization, expression in vital normal tissues, and payload and linker chemistry. Localization alone does not indicate whether a compartment contains sufficient antigen to affect treatment. PSMA is a useful caution. We detected FOLH1 in 20% of endothelial cells, but quantitative immunohistochemistry found PSMA staining in only a small minority of breast-cancer neovessels [ 32 ]. Those authors questioned the viability of PSMA-directed theranostics in this disease. A cell type can therefore be the dominant source of a low-abundance transcript without presenting a clinically meaningful antigen burden. Our study locates the RNA signal but does not quantify surface protein or predict efficacy or toxicity. The bulk and spatial examinations answered different questions. TCGA-BRCA identified targets whose total expression differed between tumor and normal tissue. It could not show whether the signal came from malignant cells. B7-H3 was higher in bulk tumor tissue but mapped mainly to endothelium, myoepithelium, and stroma in the spatial specimen. This is not a contradiction. Tumor-versus-normal contrasts are influenced by tissue composition, so we do not interpret bulk upregulation as evidence of tumor-cell specificity. Prior work defines the limits of the study's novelty. Single-cell surveys have already been used to identify non-malignant expression of CAR-T targets [ 16 ]. ADC-target catalogues are available for pan-cancer and breast cancer tissues [ 17 , 18 ], and dissociated single-cell data have been used to assess ADC target restriction in ovarian cancer [ 19 ]. B7-H3 expression in tumor endothelium and fibroblasts has been reported [ 33 ], as has PSMA expression in breast cancer neovasculature [ 31 , 32 ]. Our contribution is narrower. We assign 11 ADC-target transcripts to cell types in intact breast tissue, including the myoepithelial compartment, and assess selected targets in 2 additional specimens using another platform. The recovery of the known B7-H3 and PSMA localizations supports the approach but does not constitute a new biological discovery. Tumor epithelium occupied spatially segregated regions, apart from stromal, immune, and vascular populations (Supplementary Fig. S3). Together with the neighborhood control, this pattern makes simple transcript spillover an unlikely explanation for the B7-H3 and PSMA findings. The discovery tumor had low ESR1 and PGR expression and comparatively high ERBB2 . HER2 and TROP2 localization should therefore be interpreted within the context of their respective receptors rather than generalized across all breast cancer subtypes. Cross-specimen support was strongest for HER2 and TROP2. Their enrichment in tumor epithelium recurred in both Xenium specimens and on a second imaging platform. The invasive ductal carcinoma specimen came from a different patient, but the public metadata did not establish patient-level independence for the reference block. The evidence therefore represents recurrence across three specimens and two platforms, not three independent patients. EGFR was highest in myoepithelial cells in both Xenium specimens, showing that tumor restriction cannot be assumed for every target. B7-H3 and PSMA were absent from the targeted panel, so their localization remains based on the discovery specimen. The survival analyses provide no evidence that any target is an independent prognostic marker. Nominal associations differed between the full cohort and the complete-covariate subset and did not survive correction for or adjustment for covariates. This null result should not be read as proof that the target expression has no prognostic relevance in any subgroup. The cohort was unselected, the number of events was limited, and we deliberately avoided exploratory analyses by subtype or alternative endpoints. Translating these transcript-level maps into clinical decisions will require protein-level measurement and direct correlation with ADC efficacy and toxicity. We regard this as the central next step, rather than a peripheral caveat. A practical sequence would begin with multiplexed immunofluorescence or imaging mass cytometry on matched tissue sections, using the lineage markers applied here to reproduce the cell assignments alongside antibodies directed against the ectodomains engaged by ADCs. Simultaneous RNA and protein co-detection on the same section would then allow the transcript-to-protein relationship to be assessed cell-by-cell rather than assumed. Compartment-resolved quantitative scoring, as applied to PSMA in breast-cancer neovasculature [ 32 ], could subsequently convert localization into an estimate of antigen burden within each compartment. Clinical correlation would require complementary study designs. For efficacy, pretreatment tumor blocks from patients subsequently treated with a defined ADC could be scored separately for tumor-cell and microenvironmental target protein expression and related to objective response and progression-free survival. Assessment of toxicity would require additional evidence from relevant normal tissues and organ-specific adverse events in ADC-treated cohorts, because protein expression within the tumor microenvironment alone cannot establish on-target/off-tumor toxicity. Only outcome-linked studies of this kind can determine whether compartment-specific expression patterns such as those reported here for B7-H3 and PSMA have measurable clinical consequences. The spatial framework may also be relevant beyond ADCs. Nanoparticle and other tumor-directed delivery systems are influenced by vascular permeability, stromal barriers, and the organization of the tumor microenvironment [ 14 , 15 ]. Although these mechanisms differ from antigen-dependent ADC targeting, they reinforce the broader value of resolving delivery-relevant compartments within intact tissue. Until protein-level and outcome-linked data become available, however, the present findings should be interpreted as a hypothesis-generating guide to where such validation should be directed, not as evidence of ADC efficacy or safety. Limitations The whole-transcriptome discovery analysis is based on one tumor. HER2 and TROP2 were examined in two additional public Xenium specimens, but only one was clearly documented as a different patient. B7-H3 and PSMA were not present in the targeted validation panel. Their low-abundance stromal and vascular patterns, therefore, require confirmation in larger, patient-level cohorts across breast cancer subtypes. Cell annotations were marker-based rather than reviewed against matched histopathology. Differential expression tests also treated cells from a single specimen as independent units, which can inflate statistical confidence. Effect sizes and marker identity are more informative here than nominal cell-level P values. Public metadata did not consistently provide specimen-level sex and gender information, and these variables were not analyzed. Whole-transcriptome imaging was sparse for individual genes, limiting per-cell quantification. The bulk and survival analyses were based on a single cohort, and no signal of survival remained after adjustment. Most importantly, every target measurement was messenger RNA. ADC binding depends on the availability of an accessible cell-surface protein, whose RNA abundance cannot be measured directly. We did not assess protein localization, internalization, drug response, or toxicity. The findings are therefore descriptive and hypothesis-generating. Conclusion Single-cell spatial transcriptomics separated ADC targets enriched in tumor epithelium from targets expressed in stromal and vascular cells. HER2 and TROP2 showed the most consistent tumor enrichment across the three profiled specimens, whereas EGFR did not. These RNA-level findings should inform the design of protein-level, multi-patient validation studies. They cannot substitute for direct measurement of surface antigen or ADC activity. Compartment-resolved protein confirmation, followed by correlation with ADC response and toxicity in treated cohorts, is the necessary next step before any of these observations is applied clinically. Ethics approval and informed consent This study used only publicly available, de-identified datasets and involved no direct participant contact or new data collection. Ethical approval and informed-consent procedures for the source studies were reported in the original dataset publications. No additional ethics approval or informed consent was required for this secondary analysis. Funding This work was supported by the Ningxia Natural Science Foundation [grant numbers 2026AAC031176, 2026AAC031199 and 2025AAC030748], the National Natural Science Foundation of China [grant number 82260716], and the Regional Key Research and Development Program of the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region [grant number 2026BEG02001]. The funders had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, manuscript preparation, or the decision to submit the article for publication. Declaration of competing interest The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this article. Data and code availability All analyzed datasets are publicly available. The discovery dataset was the CosMx SMI Human Whole Transcriptome FFPE breast dataset (breast discovery release, sample S0; Bruker Spatial Biology; https://nanostring.com/products/cosmx-spatial-molecular-imager/ffpe-dataset/ ). The validation datasets were the Xenium Human Breast invasive ductal carcinoma specimen (Xenium_V1_FFPE_Human_Breast_IDC_With_Addon) and the Human Breast Cancer reference block (Xenium_FFPE_Human_Breast_Cancer_Rep1) from the 10x Genomics Datasets portal ( https://www.10xgenomics.com/datasets ). TCGA-BRCA gene expression and clinical data were obtained from the UCSC Xena TCGA hub ( https://tcga.xenahubs.net ). Analysis scripts and package versions are provided in the Supplementary_Code.zip file. Supplementary Tables S1-S7 and Fig. source data are provided as machine-readable Excel workbooks.

Biological entity Colon Experimental variable colorectal cancer (CRC) spec-5-gkvg Specimen Title TO_019 Sample preparation protocol Tonsil tissue sections were placed on SuperFrost PlusTM microscope slides (Thermo Scientific) for individual or combined Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression (10x Genomics) and COMET (Bio-Techne). For Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression analysis, SuperFrost Plus slides with FFPE tissues underwent deparaffinization, H&E staining, imaging and decrosslinking exactly according to the Visium HD FFPE Tissue Preparation Handbook (CG000684, 10x Genomics). After H&E staining, samples were imaged using the SLIDEVIEW VS200 slide scanner (ref, Evident) at 20x magnification. Visium HD Gene Expression libraries were then generated using the Visium HD, Human Transcriptome, 6.5mm reagents (PN: 1000675, 10x Genomics) and following the Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Reagent Kits User Guide (CG000685, 10x Genomics). Quality control and molarity calculations of the libraries were performed with Qubit 3.0 Fluorometer (#Q33216, Invitrogen) and 4200 Tapestation system (Agilent Technologies). Libraries were sequenced on the NovaSeq X+ 10B at paired-end 100bp. spec-12-hdqe-removable Specimen Title TO_017 Sample preparation protocol Tonsil tissue sections were placed on SuperFrost PlusTM microscope slides (Thermo Scientific) for individual or combined Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression (10x Genomics) and COMET(Bio-Techne). Sequential Immunofluorescence (SeqIF) staining was performed on FFPE tissue sections using COMET system from Lunaphore, according to standard protocol for proteomic applications (User manual – COMET, Revision: 006).
Briefly, SuperFrost Plus slides with FFPE tissue underwent deparaffinization and antigen retrieval using Dewax and HIER buffer, pH 9 (Epredia, #TA-999-DHBH) in the PT module (Epredia, ref) at 102°C for 1h, with pre-heating temperature set to 85°C and cool-end temperature to 65°C. Following antigen retrieval, slides were rinsed and kept in the Multistaining Buffer (BU06, Lunaphore) until loading them on to the instrument for SeqIF. SeqIF staining was performed on the COMET using the SPYRE Immuno-oncology Core Panel (Lunaphore) supplemented with pan-Cytokeratin antibody (ref). SeqIF protocol was set up on the COMET control software and sequential staining, imaging, and elution cycles were performed on the instrument as per manufacturer’s protocol. title: Cellular senescence in human liver under normal aging and cancer.
xenium_reason: New profiling/generation with Xenium is stated
evidence_text: Cellular senescence in human liver under normal aging and cancer. Cellular senescence, a stress-induced program causing stable cell-cycle arrest, is a hallmark of liver aging, fibrosis, and cancer. However, the cell-type-specific mechanisms, spatial organization, and cancer-associated alterations in the liver remain unclear. We profiled 43 normal human livers spanning ages and fibrosis stages using a single-cell multiome, Xenium spatial transcriptomics, and CODEX, complemented by fibrotic mouse models and 24 colorectal cancer liver metastases. We found CDKN1A+ senescent hepatocytes, fibroblasts, cholangiocytes, and endothelial cells associated with age, liver disease, or cancer. Senescence differed between aged and fibrotic livers, with similar patterns in mice. Spatially, CDKN1A+ hepatocytes localized periportally, while SERPINE1+ aging-associated hepatocytes formed spatial clusters, potentially mediated by Claudins and THBS1. Fibrotic regions contained CXCL12+ senescent fibroblasts interacting with CXCR4+ immune cells. Chemotherapy intensified senescence in hepatocytes by 5-fold relative to aging and led to unique CDKN2A+ populations. Across conditions, senescent cells shared AP-1 activation, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and apoptosis resistance, suggesting therapeutic opportunities.

title: Spatial multi-omics and single-cell transcriptomics uncover senescence-associated cellular programs during colon adenoma to cancer progression
xenium_reason: New profiling/generation with Xenium is stated
evidence_text:
Spatial multi-omics and single-cell transcriptomics uncover senescence-associated cellular programs during colon adenoma to cancer progression Colorectal cancer develops through a normal-adenoma-carcinoma sequence, yet only 5-10% of adenomas progress to malignancy, and the cellular programs governing that sequence remain poorly defined. Here we generate a spatial multi-omics atlas of human colon adenomas, combining Visium CytAssist and protein co-detection across 24 nonadvanced and advanced tubular adenomas with single-cell resolution Xenium Prime 5K profiling of 101 patient-matched normal, adenoma, and carcinoma cores from 16 patients. Integrating whole-transcriptome and 31-plex protein data identifies nine spatial clusters and two dysplastic epithelial populations that co-express stemness, proliferation, and senescence programs. These programs occupy a shared, spatially confined epithelial niche that expands from adenoma to carcinoma. Spatial analysis revealed GDF15, a senescence-associated secretory factor, mediated the coupling between senescence and stemness in advanced adenomas, and that GDF15-high epithelium locally excludes CD8+ T cells in adenoma and, more broadly, in carcinoma. These findings position senescence as a spatially instructive rather than merely tumor-suppressive program during colorectal carcinogenesis and suggest GDF15 might be a potential candidate target for cancer prevention and interception in the colon.

Statement of Significance

Spatial multi-omics identifies spatially co-localized senescence and stemness programs in dysplastic epithelium during colorectal tumorigenesis and links GDF15-associated niches to CD8-positive T-cell exclusion, nominating GDF15 for colorectal cancer prevention and interception strategies.

Explainable machine learning and multimodal single cell analysis link NR4A2 to CD8<sup>+</sup> T-cell terminal exhaustion and a CD8-adjusted prognostic signature in hepatocellular carcinoma.

Background

Terminal exhaustion of CD8+ tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes constrains the benefit of immune-checkpoint blockade in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The orphan nuclear receptor NR4A2 (Nurr1) belongs to a transcription-factor family implicated in murine T-cell exhaustion, yet its behaviour in the human HCC microenvironment has not been characterised across data modalities. We asked whether NR4A2 is specifically coupled to the terminal-exhaustion programme of human HCC CD8+ T cells, and whether that coupling is reflected in chromatin, tissue topography and bulk-tumour outcome data.

Methods

We reanalysed publicly available human HCC datasets spanning four modalities: single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq; GSE149614, GSE98638, GSE151530, GSE125449), single-cell ATAC sequencing (scATAC-seq; GSE227265), imaging-based spatial transcriptomics (10× Xenium human liver-cancer section) and bulk RNA sequencing with overall-survival annotation (TCGA-LIHC). NR4A2 was profiled across cell compartments and, at higher resolution, across CD8+ T-cell states defined from curated exhaustion, progenitor, effector and naïve gene modules. We tested NR4A2-exhaustion coupling at single-cell and pseudobulk level, examined NR4A2 motif accessibility, traced NR4A2 along a diffusion-pseudotime exhaustion axis, evaluated spatial co-localisation of exhausted CD8+ T cells with tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs), benchmarked machine-learning classifiers of the exhausted state, and compared the human NR4A2 co-expression direction with the published NR4A1/2-knockout phenotype. We additionally trained interpretable gradient-boosted-tree models with SHAP attribution to characterise the exhausted and NR4A2-high states, scored a NR4A2 co-expression regulon, related the programme to immunotherapy-relevant signatures, and modelled overall survival using a CD8-infiltration-adjusted exhaustion score.

Results

NR4A2 was broadly expressed across HCC compartments and was highest in myeloid cells rather than being T-cell restricted; at whole-compartment and bulk-tumour resolution it was not a clean exhaustion marker. At the resolution of CD8+ T-cell states, however, NR4A2 was sharply enriched in terminally exhausted cells (mean 3.62 versus 1.05; Mann-Whitney p ≈ 3.4 × 10-83) and correlated with the exhaustion module (single-cell Spearman ρ = 0.45) but not with the effector module (ρ = 0.06), arguing that NR4A2 is not a generic activation gene. NR4A2 expression increased monotonically along a diffusion-pseudotime axis toward terminal exhaustion (ρ = 0.37). In Xenium tissue, exhausted CD8+ T cells were modestly but significantly enriched in the neighbourhood of TAMs relative to other CD8+ T cells (permutation p = 0.005). The human NR4A2 co-expression direction was 83% concordant with the published NR4A1/2-knockout differential-expression direction. In bulk TCGA-LIHC, NR4A2 was lower in tumour than adjacent liver and only weakly exhaustion-correlated, consistent with hepatocyte-dominated bulk signal and reinforcing the need for compartment-resolved analysis. Interpretable machine learning attributed NR4A2-high status to an immediate-early/AP-1 activation programme, a NR4A2 co-expression regulon was selectively active in exhausted cells, and the programme tracked the T-cell-inflamed phenotype (ρ = 0.87); although raw bulk NR4A2 was non-prognostic, a CD8-infiltration-adjusted exhaustion score independently predicted shorter overall survival (hazard ratio 1.42 per standard deviation, p < 0.001).

Conclusions

A NR4A2 co-expression regulon was most active in exhausted cells; explainable modelling linked NR4A2-high status to an immediate-early/AP-1 activation programme; the programme marked immune-hot tumours; and although bulk NR4A2 was non-prognostic, a CD8-infiltration-adjusted exhaustion score was independently associated with worse overall survival (HR 1.42 per SD, p < 0.001). Across four independent data modalities, NR4A2 behaves as a resolution-dependent marker of the terminal-exhaustion programme in HCC CD8+ T cells that is spatially associated with the myeloid niche. The convergence supports NR4A2 as a candidate component of an HCC exhaustion signature and a hypothesis-generating target for functional study, while underscoring that its association is masked in bulk and whole-compartment data.
